# C13 dossier: Run-Base Shrinker (vendor-neutral pay-from-audited-savings for the application run estate)

Researched 2026-10-18 for pool P129 (US spend on offshore-delivered IT services, about $100B a year, a [my estimate] from the pool file). Tags: **[src]** read in a source; **[vendor]** a seller's own claim; **[my est.]** my arithmetic or assumption; **[unverified]** could not be confirmed. About 45 searches and fetches; several fetches were blocked (403), which I flag where it matters.

## 1. Bottom line

- **Not dead, but the upside case does not hold.** The gate's $110M upside needs about 79 clients at $1.26M each. I could not verify any of its five inputs at the level used; the share is closest (25% is documented, 30-35% is not). With evidence-anchored inputs the same arithmetic needs about 220 clients.
- **The "nobody does this" claim is wrong in spirit.** Rimini Street, the AMS vendors themselves, contingency advisers, FinOps software, and well-funded AI-SRE startups each cover a slice of the four levers. The unoccupied slot is narrower: vendor-neutral, engineering-funded, paid only from audited net reduction on the client's ledger.
- **Two new legal and structural problems the gate missed:** (a) the proposed "Big 4 audit partner co-signs the measurement protocol" may collide with SEC auditor-independence rules on contingent fees (my inference; section 7); (b) the ESCO analogy does not carry its financing mechanism across, so the 36-month receivable tail is hard to finance.
- **My read:** a real $10-25M services business with a plausible path to a protocol/data asset; a $100M outcome has roughly a 10-15% chance [my est.].

## 2. Market context and industry economics (workflow steps 0-2)

**Metrics this industry runs on:** net run-cost reduction as % of baseline; savings share %; payback months; dispute rate on baselines; contract tail; clients per year.

- Gartner puts 2026 worldwide IT services spend at about $1.87T, up 9.0% [src](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-04-22-gartner-forecasts-worldwide-it-spending-to-grow-13-point-5-percent-in-2026-totaling-6-point-31-trillion-dollars). The pool's $100B US offshore figure is an assumption of two-thirds of India's roughly $149B IT services [src](https://www.etvbharat.com/en/business/india-fy26-tech-revenues-hit-usd-315-billion-enn26022404879), not a measured number.
- Managed services is the weak part of that market: ISG shows 1H26 managed-services growth of 2.7%, the Americas down 6%, and a 2.1% full-year forecast [src](https://isg-one.com/articles/index-insider---1h26-isg-index-recap). The same recap says providers are pricing around assumed AI savings and that "neither providers nor enterprises have full visibility into how the savings will be achieved." That is the strongest single piece of why-now evidence for an independent referee.
- Value flow: client pays vendor on FTE, ticket or fixed-bid terms; Cognizant says fixed-bid and transaction-based work is now over 50% of revenue [src](https://www.aol.com/articles/cognizant-ctsh-q4-2025-earnings-151319282.html). Under fixed-bid, a ticket reduction raises the vendor's margin, not the client's saving, until a reset. Under ticket pricing, TCS itself notes that low-volume scenarios could not cover fixed costs, which is why ticket pricing struggled [src](https://www.tcs.com/insights/blogs/generative-ai-outcome-based-pricing-models-service-desk). Revenue minimums are standard and can swallow a volume reduction [src](https://www.networkworld.com/article/782328/saas-beware-of-minimum-commitments-for-outsourcing-contracts.html).
- Renegotiation is real: clients are reopening deals within 24 months, with contracts above $50M ACV under most pressure [src](https://www.hfsresearch.com/news/ai-drives-it-contract-renegotiations-within-24-months-as-pricing-models-shift/). The HFS article gives no rate. The gate's "25% a year" (a Cognizant CFO forecast) is [unverified]: I could not fetch its source (403) and found no corroboration.

## 3. Competitors: confirmed, refuted, added (steps 4-7)

| Group | Who | What they actually sell | Threat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Same promise, from the vendor | AMS majors | Self-funded transformation from ticket cuts and automation: NTT DATA claims up to 40% savings [vendor](https://ca.nttdata.com/en/-/media/assets/brochure/apps-amo-digital-transformation-fact-sheet.pdf); Mphasis a 25-30% ticket drop in a year [vendor](https://www.mphasis.com/home/services/application-services/application-management-services/case-study/logistics.html); Hexaware $1.6M saved over 3 years with 25% of tickets automated [vendor](https://hexaware.com/case-study/nextgen-application-managed-services-saves-1-6m-over-3-years-for-a-leading-us-based-employee-benefits-company/) | High: they own the data and the contract |
| Self-funding is mainstream | HFS/UST survey of 110 Global 2000 executives: 42% use self-funding as standard, 86% would start before savings are realized (UST co-produced, so promotional) [src](https://www.hfsresearch.com/?p=197112) | Proves demand and shows the incumbent already occupies the pitch | High |
| Rimini Street | 2025 revenue $421.5M (-1.7%), 3,102 clients, 88% revenue retention [src](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260219293814/en/Rimini-Street-Announces-Fiscal-Fourth-Quarter-and-Annual-2025-Financial-and-Operating-Results). Its Managed Services Optimization is a roughly five-week consulting engagement (ticket analysis, root causes, ROI model, roadmap), steered to "trusted partners like Rimini Street" [src](https://www.riministreet.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/rimini-street-rimini-consult-managed-services-optimization-datasheet.pdf) | Feeder into its own managed services. The gate's "unlimited-ticket model" is not in the datasheet I read [unverified]; I found no fee tied to savings | Medium |
| Contingency advisers | Redress Compliance: 25% of savings beyond the vendor's best offer, no savings no fee, 10-40% typical contract-value movement [vendor](https://redresscompliance.com/pay-from-savings); a PE sponsor case: $100M removed across 14 portfolio companies in 30 months, 60%+ from five vendors [vendor](https://redresscompliance.com/case-study-pe-portfolio-software-spend-reduction-100m) | Licence and contract levers (lever 4 and part of 1) and a PE channel, with no engineering | High on licences |
| Governance | ISG GovernX, Avasant AvaSense (invoice, credit and earn-back review) [src via gate](https://avasant.com/what-we-do/contract-supplier-governance/) | Measurement without engineering | Medium |
| Software, % of savings | ProsperOps: fee is a share of realized savings, rate set per contract; a third party estimates 30-35% [unverified](https://spendark.com/blog/prosperops-alternative/); manages about $6B of cloud spend, sold to Flexera in Jan 2026 [src](https://pulse2.com/h-i-g-growth-partners-sells-prosperops-to-flexera-in-finops-automation-exit) | Shows private buyers pay a percentage of savings; no ARR or sale price disclosed | Analog |
| SaaS and portfolio tools | Zylo reports 46% of licences unused and $19.8M waste per company [vendor](https://zylo.com/blog/how-much-wasted-on-saas-spend); SoftwareOne sells application portfolio consolidation [src](https://www.softwareone.com/en/asset-management/application-portfolio-consolidation-services) | Lever 1 for SaaS is already a software category | Medium |
| AI-native, repeat incidents | Resolve AI ($125M Series A at $1B, ~$4M ARR at the time) [src](https://techcrunch.com/2025/12/19/ex-splunk-execs-startup-resolve-ai-hits-1-billion-valuation-with-series-a); Traversal ($48M) [src](https://siliconangle.com/2025/06/18/traversal-launches-48m-tackle-site-reliability-observability-ai/); DataAgent ($10M pre-seed, Kubernetes remediation, not legacy apps) [src](https://thesaasnews.com/news/dataagent-raises-10m-pre-seed); Cleric [src](https://pulse2.com/cleric-4-3-million-raised-and-autonomous-ai-site-reliability-engineer-unveiled) | Lever 2's engineering is sold as software, so a client can buy it without paying 35% | High, and new to the gate |
| AI-native, SAP and legacy | Tessera Labs ($60M Series A; SAP upgrades and custom-code analysis; pricing not stated) [src](https://a16z.com/announcement/investing-in-tessera-labs/); Kodesage, Hypercubic (seed stage, per the pool file) | Wedge 1 (SAP custom code) | Medium |
| Free substitutes | SAP's own Custom Code Migration app, ABAP Test Cockpit, and SCMON/UPL usage logging [src](https://www.consilio-gmbh.de/en/trendblog/custom-code-fit-for-sap-s-4hana-analyze-adapt-benefit) | The analysis step of the SAP wedge costs nothing | Medium |

**No "ESCO for IT" found.** A direct search found only energy-based performance contracts used to fund IT, and nothing for IT run costs. The slot is open, but the open slot may be open because the economics are hard (sections 4 and 6), not because nobody thought of it.

## 4. Bottom-up market and the upside assumptions

**Reachable payers.** Tier counts are global and for one vendor at a time: TCS had 66 clients above $100M and 139 above $50M at Q4 FY26 [src](https://arihantresearch.arihantcapital.com/Mumbai_Research/TCS_Result_Update_Q4FY26.pdf); Infosys's $50M+ and $100M+ cohorts each grew by three in FY26 per a call transcript that may be garbled [src](https://www.infosys.com/investors/reports-filings/quarterly-results/2025-2026/q4/documents/transcripts/earningscall.pdf). Clients overlap across vendors, offshore AMS is only part of a client's vendor spend, and the US is a fraction. My estimate is **300-600 US enterprises** with $30M+ of offshore run spend [my est.; no source counts them]. The gate's 79 clients is therefore **13-26% of reachable payers**, at or over the lessons file's 20% "heroic share" line.

**Each upside input, tested:**

| Input (gate) | Best evidence | Holds? |
|---|---|---|
| Savings share 30-35% (idea said 30-50%) | Contingency advisers quote 25% [vendor](https://redresscompliance.com/pay-from-savings); ProsperOps 30-35% is a third-party guess. Nothing supports 50% | 25-30% plausible; 35% a stretch; 50% unsupported |
| 12% reduction of run base in 3 years | Only vendor claims: Deloitte 15-20% on application rationalization, "not always guaranteed" [vendor](https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone3/us/en/docs/alliances/2025/deloitte-google-cloud-health-care-self-funding-value-proposition.pdf); the vendor cases above. Ticket cuts do not convert 1:1 because of fixed-bid terms and minimums (section 2) | Untested. 5-8% is defensible; 12% needs an unsourced best case |
| Dead custom code lever (SAP) | "60-75% never called" is one author's estimate with no method [src](https://blog.sap-press.com/how-to-evaluate-custom-code-usage-data-ahead-of-an-sap-s4hana-migration); a self-reported cleanup removed 17% of a codebase after 14 months of usage data, below its own expectation [unverified](https://no.linkedin.com/in/endre-jonassen-48049b46). Removed code saves little run cost unless a conversion fee or licence falls with it | Weak as a standalone $ lever |
| $30M run base per client | Only the pool's assumption | Plausible only for the top few hundred buyers |
| 79 clients in 6-7 years | Rimini Street, the closest "cheaper than the incumbent" analog, has about 3,100 clients and its 2025 revenue fell 1.7% | Aggressive for a CFO-signed, audit-reviewed deal |

**Scenario arithmetic** (revenue per client = base x reduction x share) [my est.]:
- Gate case: $30M x 12% x 35% = $1.26M, so 79 clients for $100M.
- Evidence-anchored: $30M x 6% x 25% = $0.45M, so about 222 clients (37-74% of reachable payers).
- Large-base variant: if the savings base is the client's whole application run bill (labor, licences, hosting) at $100M, then 8% x 30% = $2.4M, so about 42 clients. This is the most plausible path to $100M, and it depends on lever 1 and lever 4 (client-controlled lines), where Redress-style advisers and SaaS tools already compete on the same dollars.

## 5. Demand and willingness to pay

- **For:** self-funded transformation is standard or selective at 80% of surveyed enterprises, though the survey is vendor-co-produced (section 3). Providers are re-pricing on unverifiable AI assumptions (ISG, section 2). PE sponsors do pay for portfolio-wide cost programs (the Redress case, though its fee was undisclosed). Broadcom's VMware repricing forces right-sizing spend: a survey reports 59% of customers saw increases above 25% and only 4% fully migrated (secondary coverage; I did not open the primary survey) [src](https://petri.com/vmware-pricing-fears-enterprise-virtualization-shift/). SAP ECC mainstream maintenance ends 31 Dec 2027 with paid extension to 2030 (sources conflict on the extension premium, from 2 points to about 12%; the "39% still on ECC" figure is from an adviser blog) [src](https://www.crowe.com/id/insights/sap-ecc-support-ends-in-2027-what-leaders-should-do).
- **Against:** I found no RFP, tender or published contract for third-party, share-of-savings application-run reduction. Disputes over gainshare baselines are documented: Somerset County Council's gainshare with Southwest One ended in a settlement after the provider's savings claims were rejected [src](https://www.localgovernmentlawyer.co.uk/litigation-and-enforcement/311-litigation-features/13717-council-and-outsourcing-provider-settle-multi-million-pound-dispute), and Sprint and IBM fought over the productivity formula [src](https://www.fierce-network.com/wireless/sprint-sues-ibm-over-outsourcing-contract).
- **Who signs:** CIO and CFO; the PE operating partner is the forcing function (inference). The person who owns the run budget is also the person whose vendor is being cut, which slows deals.

## 6. Unit economics, analogs and capital

- **ESCO scale and shape.** LBNL: US ESCO revenue $10.7B in 2024; K-12 and public agencies about $5B (47%); commercial and industrial only 6%, mostly design-build rather than performance contracting; M&V on about 80% of projects; real growth 56% since 2014 [src](https://www.facilitiesdive.com/news/energy-services-companies-are-becoming-a-15b-industry/831664/). The whole US ESCO industry is $10.7B of revenue and mostly public-sector, while the gate's pool view implies one new IT category capturing a $1.68B annual fee pool ($40B x 12% x 35%).
- **Public ESCO comp.** Ameresco: 2025 revenue $1,932.1M, net income $44.3M (2.3%), adjusted EBITDA $237.2M (12.3%), Q4 gross margin 16.2%, backlog over $5B [src](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260302626462/en/Ameresco-Reports-Fourth-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Financial-Results). The model scales but earns thin margins on a heavy balance sheet.
- **Contingency recovery comps.** PRGX, the scaled contingency-fee auditor, was taken private for about $195M in 2021 [src](https://www.sheppard.com/news-and-events/press-releases/sheppard-advises-ardian-in-acquistion-of-prgx-for-195-million). Vaudit's own pages disagree ($50M+ versus $100M+ lifetime recoveries; "no percentage" versus "success fee") [vendor](https://www.vaudit.com/vendor-audit-native). The one scaled public contingency-fee auditor selling for about $195M is a ceiling signal, not proof.
- **Financing gap.** In ESCO deals the customer finances through loans, leases and bonds [src](https://www.facilitiesdive.com/news/energy-services-companies-are-becoming-a-15b-industry/831664/) while the ESCO guarantees the savings [src](https://goodwindco.in/blog/energy-service-company-esco/). A private enterprise will not issue tax-exempt-style debt for IT savings, so the Shrinker would carry the performance risk and a receivable that is variable and disputable. Rough capital [my est.]: $1.0-1.5M of engineering per client up front, 12-15 new clients a year, 18-month payback, so $30-70M of peak outlay before receivables turn. Lenders will treat contingent receivables as equity-like.
- **Accounting.** Shared savings is variable consideration; revenue is recognized only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable [src](https://www.revenuehub.org/variable-consideration-constraint/), so reported revenue lags cash and invites auditor scrutiny [src](https://bakertilly.com/insights/the-revenue-recognition-transition-determining-the-transaction-price).

## 7. Legal, regulatory and liability landscape

1. **Auditor independence (new).** SEC Rule 2-01(c)(5) makes an accountant non-independent if it provides services to an audit client for a contingent fee or receives one from it; staff treat it as a direct financial interest, with no materiality test, and affiliates count [src](https://www.sec.gov/info/accountants/noaction/aapwc.htm). EY was sanctioned in 2021 for contingent-fee work for an audit client [src](https://www.sec.gov/files/litigation/admin/2021/34-93749.pdf). PCAOB Rule 3521 adds indirect fees. The gate's idea of a Big 4 audit partner co-signing the protocol must avoid any client for which that firm is the auditor, and a business relationship with a contingent-fee vendor could itself raise independence questions [my inference; verify with counsel]. Cleaner alternatives: a non-auditor firm, a standards-body model like IPMVP, or Internal Audit only.
2. **Contract access.** Minimum revenue commitments, fixed-bid pricing and vendor-held ITSM data can block or erase vendor-line savings (section 2). Lever 1 and lever 4 avoid this by cutting client-owned invoices.
3. **Retirement liability.** Retiring an application requires validated extracts, preserved metadata, retention schedules and legal holds, and SOX 404 evidence may be needed for years after [vendor-written guide](https://dev.to/sam_mitchell_ee4afb8d68c3/application-retirement-the-complete-guide-to-retiring-legacy-applications-without-losing-critical-5b2i). A shutdown that breaks a hidden dependency is an operational loss with the Shrinker's name on it. I found no standard indemnity or insurance for this [gap]; liability caps and E&O cover must be priced in.
4. **No statute prohibits** third-party share-of-savings IT fees that I found; the risks are contractual and accounting, not regulatory.

## 8. Is the why-now real?

Partly. The pricing reset is real and verified: ISG's unverifiable AI-savings assumptions, HFS's 24-month renegotiations, and flat managed-services growth. But the same shock cuts against the product in two ways. (1) Vendors are cutting their own prices; if clients win 25-30% cuts at renegotiation (Persistent's CEO, per the idea file; not re-verified) a third party earning on a baseline "beyond contract pass-through" may have little left to claim. (2) AI-SRE and ticket-deflection tooling is becoming cheap software ($1B-valuation Resolve AI), so engineering for lever 2 may be bought outright. The SAP deadline is soft (extension to 2030), and VMware pressure feeds licence advisers first.

## 9. Synthesis

**Moats.** Counter-positioning against AMS vendors: Moderate, and only where the Shrinker never needs vendor cooperation. A cross-client root-cause and retirement library: Moderate, but AI-SRE vendors learn across clients too. An auditor-accepted protocol: potentially Strong, but unproven and legally fragile (section 7). Switching costs: Weak after the 36-month tail, with receivable finance the real barrier to entry.

**Structural vulnerabilities:** baseline disputes; private CFOs unwilling to hand 25-35% of savings to a third party when advisers charge 25% for less risk; and the savings pool shrinking as vendors self-deflate.

| Scenario | Probability [my est.] | Annual revenue, year 6-7 | Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bull | 12% | $80-110M | Large-base variant works; protocol becomes a standard; PE channel mandates it |
| Base | 38% | $12-30M | 30-60 clients, mostly lever 1 and 4, licence-adviser overlap |
| Bear | 50% | under $8M | Baseline disputes, CFOs cap share near 20%, AI-SRE tools substitute |

**Tests that would change my mind (60-90 days):** (1) three written LOIs from CFOs accepting a share of 30% or more on client-controlled lines; (2) minimum-commitment, reset and data-custody clauses read in five real MSAs; (3) a repeat-ticket heatmap showing at least 6% addressable fee reduction on unit-priced contracts (the gate's kill line, which I endorse); (4) written acceptance of the measurement method from one Internal Audit group; (5) a counsel opinion on independence with a named Big 4 firm; (6) a count of US enterprises with $30M+ of offshore run spend from two former AMS delivery heads, to replace my 300-600 guess.

**Pivot note.** The largest reachable pool I found is the client-controlled application run bill (licences, hosting, retirement), not the vendor-labor pool. That moves the idea toward the Redress and SoftwareOne pool with engineering funding as the difference. That is a real wedge, but a smaller and more contested one than the pitch implies.

# C15 Dossier: Hot-Spot Contract (capitated root-cause care for the costliest homes)

Date: 2026-10-18. Pool P003, England social landlords' repairs. About 55 searches and fetches. Tags: [V] = read on the page; [S] = search-result summary only, page not read or blocked; [A] = my arithmetic or assumption. GBP/USD 1.30.

## 1. Bottom line

**Verdict: weak, leaning kill as a $100M business. Median about $13M, upside about $58M (5-7 year revenue). The gate's "strong, $20M / $100M" does not survive.** The core observation (repair demand is skewed) is real. The business built on it fails on seven counts:

1. Whole-stock "price per property" contracts already take capitated repair risk, and incumbents are locked in until 2031-36 (section 2).
2. The $100M path needs about a third of all reachable large landlords to hand over 100% of their worst homes (section 3).
3. Pricing at 80% of trailing cost collides with a repair cost curve rising 13-14% a year. The fee basis is gone in about two years without indexation (section 5).
4. The idea's accounting "earned secret" is wrong for the regulator's own metric (section 8).
5. The worst homes are often negative-value assets that boards sell or regenerate, not contract out (section 2).
6. The cross-landlord dataset is not cornered, because Mobysoft already sells it (sections 2 and 8).
7. It needs tens of millions of risk capital and the stop-loss product I could not find (sections 5 and 6).

The kill test (top 5% of homes carry at least 15% of repair spend) is still unrun. I found no published top-5% split. Closest data: section 3.

## 2. Competitors: gate list confirmed, and what it missed

| Player | Finding | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Mobysoft RepairSense | Confirmed. Vendor claims "over 7 million repair jobs" and "up to 35% reduction in avoidable repairs" [V]. Gloucester City Homes: 25% fewer repeat visits, GBP42,000 saved in six months [V]. Contract values GBP97k-276k a year (Flagship GBP109,800 [S]). | [vendor](https://platform.softwareone.com/product/repairsense/PCP-2724-7109), [GCH](https://www.housing-technology.com/gch-slashes-repeat-repairs-with-mobysoft/), [notice](https://www.contractsfinder.service.gov.uk/Notice/57151f81-c772-43ae-92be-0cc6d048f311) |
| Switchee Mould iQ | Confirmed. GBP6.5M (2023) [V] plus GBP5M (2024) raised; Mould iQ launched with three housing associations covering 92,000 homes [S]. Vendor-reported only: Fairhive "prevented an estimated GBP209,000 in disrepair costs" [S]. | [launch](https://switchee.com/mould-iq-launch), [2024 round](https://tech.eu/2024/07/10/switchee-granted-ps5m-to-tackle-mould-in-british-social-housing/), [case](https://switchee.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Case-study-Citizen-Mould.pdf) |
| Plentific | Confirmed. $100M Series C (Aug 2021), about $137-140M total. Marketplace, no repair risk. | [round](https://globalventuring.com/corporate/plentific-builds-100m-series-c/?format=md) |
| Primes on price-per-property | **Missed by the gate as a competitor.** Mears-Thurrock: GBP240M, GBP24M a year, 5+5 years from 1 July 2026, covering all reactive repairs, planned, voids and general build [S]. Mears: GBP1,135.5M revenue, 5.7% margin, "near-100%" retention, GBP4.0bn order book, GBP250M Cross Keys deal over 10 years [S]. Cardo-Dacorum: 10 years from July 2026, GBP395-457M [S]. | [Mears](https://www.lse.co.uk/rns/MER.PL/contract-award-uf851g9xbtbny72.html), [FY25](https://www.lse.co.uk/rns/MER.PL/preliminary-results-m0xef2otfifb3wu.html), [Dacorum](https://www.theconstructionindex.co.uk/news/view/dacorum-keeps-cardo-on-for-maintenance-work) |
| Frameworks with disrepair lots | PfH GBP480M framework: four lots (one GBP180M, three GBP100M) incl. disrepair works; 12 firms in all major lots, 75 suppliers overall; term to about 2030 [V]. Riverside GBP657M Total Disrepair Solutions, 12 regional lots, to about 2029 [S]. | [PfH](https://www.constructionenquirer.com/2026/07/22/pfh-names-winners-on-480m-repairs-and-disrepair-deal/), [Riverside](https://labmonline.co.uk/?p=34808) |
| In-house | Basildon takes repairs to a DLO when Morgan Sindall ends 30 Jun 2026 [S]; Ashford insourced after Equans gave notice (HQN projected GBP500k a year saving) [S]; Cheshire West took housing back early after ForHousing cited rising "number and cost of day-to-day repairs" [V]. | [Basildon](https://basildon.gov.uk/article/10853/In-the-News-Basildon-Council-confirms-future-of-housing-repairs-service), [Ashford](https://ashford.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s25062/Housing%20Repairs%20Contract.pdf), [CWAC](https://www.cheshirewestandchester.gov.uk/news/council-housing-changes-brought-forward-to-april-2026) |
| Ventilation makers | Vent-Axia and Aereco partner with landlords (Citizen, Southwark) [S]. Envirovent's 260-home study found nearly half showed some mould and that resident behaviour is not the main fix [S]. | [study](https://www.envirovent.com/sectors/councils-and-housing-associations/breaking-the-mould) |
| Insurance-backed guarantees | Damp-proofing already comes with insurer-backed guarantees (PCA scheme) [S]. | [PCA member](https://www.wisepropertycare.com/about-us/guarantees/) |

**Not found:** any firm selling a worst-cohort carve-out with capitated risk. Absence in about ten targeted searches is weak evidence, but it matches the gate.

**Why the carve-out is hard to sell.** Price-per-property is old and normal: St Albans pays "a fixed price for each property every year" on a roughly GBP90M, 15-year deal [S], and Thurrock's own 2015 policy refers to a "Per Annum Price per Property Contract" [V]. A prime on such a contract already carries the hot-spot cost and is already paid to fix root causes. It would see a carve-out as cherry-picking its upside, and its exclusivity clause likely forbids it. Only landlords on visit-priced schedule-of-rates contracts are obvious targets, and I found no data on how many remain.

**The hot spots are often an asset decision.** Landlords test each home's 30-year net present value and normally dispose of negative ones. Southwark's Savills survey found over 4,000 homes below zero; Haringey about 500 (3.4% of stock); the Northern Ireland Housing Executive 44% of stock in negative-average groups [S]. A board's answer for the worst homes is often sell or regenerate. [Southwark](https://www.southwarknews.co.uk/news/your-home-is-worth-less-than-nothing-council-report-evaluates-southwark-properties/), [Haringey](https://www.minutes.haringey.gov.uk/documents/s88245/Stock%20Investment_Oct%2016%20App2%20Options%20Appraisal%20v1%200.pdf).

## 3. Bottom-up market

- Stock: 4.1M social-rented households in 2024-25 [V] ([EHS](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6930595d4bedc0e762303ffa/2024-25_EHS_Headline_Report.pdf)); the idea used 4.4M. A 5% cohort is about 205,000-220,000 homes.
- Reachable payers: the 19 largest private providers hold 42% of units, and 200 groups hold over 96% [V] ([RSH](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/regulator-of-social-housing-2025-global-accounts-published)). The 40th largest association has about 36,000 homes [S] ([Housing Today](https://www.housingtoday.co.uk/news/onward-homes-appoints-new-chief-executive/5139808.article)). I could not find a count above 25,000 homes; my estimate is about 45-55 including a few big councils [A].
- Spend per home is the weak link. Whole-stock total-asset contracts run about GBP2,240 per home a year (Dacorum GBP23.5M on 10,500 homes [S]; Thurrock GBP24M on about 10,000 [A]), but that includes planned and compliance work. Responsive plus voids was GBP595 per property in 2019-20 (HouseMark via [Broxtowe](https://democracy.broxtowe.gov.uk/documents/s11707/7.1%20NOTE%20Housemark%20Committee%20Report%202.2.21%20003.pdf)). The idea's GBP2,800 "four times average" for the cohort is an unsourced assumption [A].
- Sector scale: GBP10bn of repairs and maintenance in 2024/25, GBP3.9bn capitalised [V] ([RSH](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/regulator-of-social-housing-2025-global-accounts-published)). The cohort pool is about GBP570-620M a year [A], all of it money landlords already spend.

**$100M path.** GBP77M needs about 35,000 homes at GBP2,200. If cohorts run about 2,000 homes per 40,000-home landlord, that is about 17 landlords each handing over 100% of their hot spots. At 45-55 reachable landlords, that is 30-40% of the payer set. The gate counted it as 16% of the national cohort. I count it as heroic share by the lessons' own rule (over 20%).

**Skew evidence, and what it can and cannot support.**
- Thurrock (data Aug 2013-Jul 2014): 3.7 repairs per home against a national 2.5. Of 10,315 homes, 5,450 had two or fewer repairs, 2,072 had three to four, and **2,793 (27%) had five or more**, out of about 38,000 jobs [V]. If the low band averaged 1.2-2.0 repairs, the 5+ band produced roughly 52-64% of jobs [A]. The council attributed this to "particular issues with the property" and to resident approach, both. [Thurrock policy](https://democracy.thurrock.gov.uk/documents/s2411/Responsive%20Repairs%20and%20Maintenance%20Policy.pdf).
- Leicester: 9,007 homes with four or more repairs in 2019-20, GBP88.07 average per repair [S] (page blocked to me).
- The "80% of repairs on 20% of stock" figure is from 2007 Oxford minutes citing KPMG [S]; I could not retrieve the source.
- A 2022 case study of one association found repair costs heavily right-skewed [S] ([paper](https://research.polyu.edu.hk/en/publications/analysis-and-modelling-of-social-housing-repair-and-maintenance-c/)).
- Reading: concentration is broad (a quarter of homes), not a sharp 5% tail. These are job counts from one council, 12 years old; they are consistent with a 15-25% top-5% share but do not prove it.

## 4. Demand and willingness to pay

**Real:** landlords pay for bulk disrepair work (Riverside, PfH lots above). Damp and mould spend is visible: Wigan GBP2M in 2025/26 ([FOI](https://www.wigan.gov.uk/Docs/PDF/Council/Disclosure-Logs/2025/18547.pdf)), InCommunities about GBP3M ([RNS](https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/rns/incommunities-treasury-plc--94bd/half-year-financial-report/9290482)). The Ombudsman says [S] repairs are 45% of complaints, complaints about substandard conditions rose 474% in five years, and repeat failures come from "temporary fixes rather than permanent repairs" and poor diagnosis ([Repairing Trust](https://www.housing-ombudsman.org.uk/2025/05/29/call-for-national-tenant-body-and-funding-review/)). Only 4% of landlords call themselves "very prepared" for phase 2 [S] ([Housing Today](https://www.housingtoday.co.uk/news/next-phase-of-awaabs-law-to-come-into-force-in-november/5143162.article)).

**Not shown:** anyone paying for risk transfer on a cohort. Demand is for works and software, not capitation.

**The disrepair "second payer line" is small and concentrated.** 78 councils and 3 associations spent about GBP25M in 2024, with claims up from 1,829 to 8,999 a year ([Legal Futures](https://www.legalfutures.co.uk/latest-news/foi-data-shows-big-rises-in-housing-disrepair-claims-and-costs)). Hackney paid GBP1M compensation plus GBP3.6M claimant legal fees on 508 claims ([Hackney Citizen](https://www.hackneycitizen.co.uk/2025/06/27/town-hall-legal-costs-disrepair-past-year/)). Lambeth's claimed GBP15.4M of 2025/26 legal costs plus a GBP19.7M provision comes from a party press release ([Lib Dems](https://fleet.libdems.org.uk/001b000003cug4e/news/article/lib-dems-reveal-shocking-cost-of-housing-disrepair-in-lambeth)); the FOI figure is GBP8.4M of damages over five years ([Brixton Buzz](https://www.brixtonbuzz.com/2026/05/lambeth-council-pays-out-more-than-8-4m-in-housing-disrepair-claims-as-london-payouts-top-31-million/)). Nationally this is tens of millions, mostly London. Claimant costs stay uncapped until at least October 2028 ([Anthony Collins](https://blog.anthonycollins.com/post/102kq77/disrepair-claims-fixed-recoverable-costs-exemption-extended-to-2028)).

**Landlord's gain:** 20% of GBP2,800 is about GBP560 a home a year, or GBP1.1M on a 2,000-home cohort [A], plus avoided claims. Real, but small next to a 5-10 year lock-in and a Procurement Act process.

**Signer:** Finance Director or Director of Assets, with board approval. Sector cash interest cover was 59% in the quarter to June 2026, and the regulator is watching covenants ([RSH Q1](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/rsh-publishes-its-quarterly-survey-for-q1-april-to-june-2026)). That squeezes the capital for root-cause works a capitation depends on.

## 5. Unit economics and analogs

Model per cohort home [A]: trailing cost GBP2,800 (idea); fee 80% = GBP2,240; overhead, data and insurance 12% of fee (GBP270); root-cause works GBP2,000 amortised over five years (GBP400 a year). For scale, current damp cases cost GBP1,150 per case at Stevenage ([minutes](https://democracy.stevenage.gov.uk/mgAi.aspx?ID=18381)) and GBP1,480 per property at Redditch ([report](https://moderngovwebpublic.redditchbc.gov.uk/documents/s53486/Damp%20and%20Mould%20Committe%20Report%20AWR%20final%20covering%20report.pdf)); roofs and structure cost more.

| Cut in recurring cost | Margin if provider funds the fix | Margin if landlord funds the fix |
|---|---|---|
| 25% (analytics-level, as at Gloucester) | -GBP530 a home, -24% | -GBP130, -6% |
| 40% | -GBP110, -5% | +GBP290, +13% |
| 60% | +GBP450, +20% | +GBP850, +38% |

Break-even needs a 44% cut when the provider funds the fix and 30% when the landlord does. The idea's 12-18% margin needs 40-60% cuts. The only measured cut I found is 25% on repeat visits from analytics alone, a vendor case ([GCH](https://www.housing-technology.com/gch-slashes-repeat-repairs-with-mobysoft/)). Mobysoft's "up to 35%" and Switchee's results are unmeasured vendor claims.

**Cost trend breaks the 80% price.** Sector repairs spend was GBP9.7bn over the last 12 months and is forecast at GBP11.1bn for the next, +14% ([RSH](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/rsh-publishes-its-quarterly-survey-for-q1-april-to-june-2026)); 2024/25 was +13%. At 13%, 80% of trailing cost is about 102% of true cost two years on [A]. The fee needs indexation and a volume re-opener, which fixed-price buyers resist. ForHousing's early exit is the live warning: it cited rising "number and cost" of repairs under a 2017 fixed arrangement.

**Analogs.** Managed-care capitation is the idea's model. It is capital-hungry and unforgiving: Cano Health filed Chapter 11 in February 2024 with about $1.2bn of assets against $1.4bn of debt, tied to capitated Medicare Advantage ([Healthcare Finance](https://www.healthcarefinancenews.com/news/cano-health-files-chapter-11-bankruptcy)); CVS paid $10.6bn for Oak Street ([Fierce](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/providers/cvs-closes-106b-acquisition-oak-street-health-expand-primary-care-footprint)), but I found no post-deal profitability. Closest in-sector benchmark: Mears earns 5.7% on GBP1.1bn.

**Capital [A].** At 35,000 homes: first-loss buffer about 10% of a GBP98M cost base, roughly GBP10M; provider-funded fixes up to GBP70M over six years (about GBP12M a year); plus bonds and professional indemnity. Pilot scale: a 500-home cohort is GBP1.1M of fee and about GBP1M of fix spend. Total: GBP20-40M of risk capital by year five. That is balance-sheet business, not venture software.

## 6. Regulatory and liability

- **FSMA.** The FCA treats a seller's warranty matching its usual quality obligations as unlikely to be insurance, but one given by someone other than the seller, or "significantly more extensive in content, scope or duration", as likely insurance; and where the event happens regardless of the provider's work quality it may be insurance ([PERG 6.7](https://handbook.fca.org.uk/handbook/perg6/perg6s7); [Freeths 2026](https://www.freeths.co.uk/insights-events/legal-articles/2026/warranty-service-contract-or-insurance-navigating-the-regulatory-landscape-for-product-protection-arrangements/)). A capitated service where the provider does every repair resembles St Albans-style pricing and is likely fine. The gate is right that the five-year uncapped guarantee is the risk. Stop-loss for repair-cost aggregates: I found no product, and insurers exclude gradual damage [S, via gate].
- **Procurement Act 2023.** Registered providers are contracting authorities ([PfH](https://www.procurementforhousing.co.uk/article/is-your-housing-association-subject-to-the-procurement-act-2023)). The services threshold is GBP207,720 including VAT from 1 January 2026 ([Bevan Brittan](https://www.bevanbrittan.com/insights/articles/2025/procurement-updated-thresholds-for-january-2026-published/), [S]). A 500-home pilot at about GBP1.1M a year is over it, so even a pilot needs a compliant route.
- **Duty stays with the landlord.** The s10A implied term sits on the landlord, with damages and specific performance in the County Court ([Clyde & Co](https://www.clydeco.com/en/insights/2026/08/awaab-s-law-phase-2-the-next-compliance-challenge)). A contractor can only sit behind an indemnity. Litigation needs SRA-regulated lawyers.

## 7. Why-now

**Real:** phase 2 regulations were laid 13 July 2026 and start 30 November 2026, adding electrical, falls, fire and explosion, excess cold and heat, structural and hygiene hazards ([CIH](https://www.cih.org/news/second-phase-of-awaabs-law-laid-before-parliament/), [gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/awaabs-law-phase-2-guidance-for-social-housing-landlords/awaabs-law-phase-2-guidance-for-social-landlords)). Clyde & Co expect a "significant increase in claims activity".

**Cuts against the idea:** the same shock raises the cost basis the fee is set from, drives insourcing (Basildon, Cheshire West), and is already being absorbed by framework disrepair lots. The one-off electrical catch-up deadline is 1 November 2026.

## 8. Upside-case assumptions: tested

| Gate assumption | Result |
|---|---|
| Top 5% carry at least 25% of spend | Unproven. Thurrock is consistent with fat-tail concentration but is old, count-based and half tenant-driven. |
| 15-20 landlords hand over 1,500-2,500 homes each within six years | Weak. No precedent for a cohort carve-out; price-per-property incumbents locked to 2031-36; landlords insourcing; each contract of about GBP4.5M a year is a flexible-procedure tender. |
| Reinsurer prices the tail on a shared dataset | No product found. Mobysoft already holds a multi-landlord repair dataset (7M jobs claimed) and sells analytics for under GBP300k a year, so the data is not cornered. |
| Framework call-off avoids 12-18 month tenders | Mostly closed: PfH's winners are named and Riverside's term runs to about 2029. A newcomer must subcontract to a winner, making the prime channel and competitor. |
| Capitalising a fix lifts the EBITDA-MRI covenant | **Wrong for EBITDA-MRI**, which deducts capitalised major repairs; it helps only plain-EBITDA covenants, which many providers have moved to ([Chatham](https://www.chathamfinancial.com/insights/covenant-trends-in-the-uk-social-housing-sector)). |

Realistic range [A]: median 3 landlords x 1,500 homes = 4,500 homes = about GBP10M (about $13M); upside 10 landlords x 2,000 homes = 20,000 homes = about GBP45M (about $58M). $100M needs the 17-landlord case.

## 9. What would change my mind, and gaps

**Change my mind:** (a) job-level data from three landlords with the top 5% at 25% or more of cost; (b) a 100-home pilot with a measured cost cut of 45% or more; (c) two schedule-of-rates landlords with written carve-out clauses; (d) a stop-loss quote; (e) a prime willing to white-label.

**Gaps:** no top-5% cost split exists publicly; mix of schedule-of-rates versus price-per-property contracts unknown; Leicester, Oxford, Ashford and Riverside source pages were blocked or unreadable (marked [S]); the Thurrock and Dacorum home counts are dated or unconfirmed; I did not read the full 2022 skew paper; the Lambeth cost figures conflict; I found no damp-and-mould cover or repair stop-loss product, which is absence of evidence only.

Vendors and rivals are moving to fixed-price, outcome-based and productivity-commitment terms. Cognizant says fixed-bid and outcome work is now over 50% of revenue. Rimini Street sells Rimini Manage on a fixed-price, unlimited-ticket model. Rimini also argues in public that time-and-materials AMS has 'no provision for root cause problem management', which is this idea's exact thesis, voiced by a vendor with 3,100 clients. Sourcing advisers are telling buyers to demand front-loaded productivity commitments and a share of the gain at renewal. ISG's Q2 2026 data shows Americas managed-services ACV down 12% to $5.2B, with IT outsourcing down 23% 'led by' application development and maintenance. Industry AI deflation is quoted at 2-5% a year, and a TCS leader reportedly says 10-15% can be committed from day one (unattributed). The gate defines the baseline as 'contract-guaranteed AI pass-through', so the Shrinker only earns beyond what the vendor already concedes. Its 6-12% headroom over 3 years is the same size as the discount the client wins anyway by renegotiating. Under fixed-bid contracts a ticket cut raises the vendor's margin, not the client's saving, until the baseline resets. On the vendor-labor lever the client's real alternative is 'renegotiate or rebid to a fixed-price vendor', which costs 0% of savings.

The target buyers have the engineering capacity and the same AI tools, and the 'fund it on spec' premise argues for in-sourcing. On 13 October 2026 Citi's CEO tied a 30% year-on-year drop in technology-vendor spend to AI-assisted insourcing, with about 14,000 engineers on Devin. A client with $20M or more of offshore run spend is exactly the profile that can do this. GitHub's own billing team uses the Copilot coding agent to burn down tech debt continuously. AWS Transform custom has generally available codebase analysis (March 2026) that produces a technical-debt report, free assessment, and no-cost AWS-managed .NET transformations. Datadog's Bits AI SRE costs roughly $6.50 per investigation on its credit model, which is a cost estimate and not a measured result. The Shrinker's pitch (AI makes root-cause fixes and dead-code deletion cheap) means the one-time engineering is a falling-cost commodity. A CFO asked to pay 30-35% of savings for 36 months on a one-time fix, while the cost of doing it falls every quarter, will cap the share, buy the tooling, or do it after year one. Evidence for large-scale in-house dead-code deletion beyond Citi and GitHub is thin, so this is a strong directional threat and not yet a measured one.

The client-controlled levers (zombie apps, licences, right-sizing), which the gate says to lead with, are exactly where platform incumbents and contingency advisers already sit. Redress Compliance offers 25% of savings with no fee if no savings, and claims a $100M cut across 14 PE portfolio companies (vendor claim). Flexera bought ProsperOps and Chaos Genius in January 2026 and sells application rationalization. LeanIX (SAP) feeds Apptio (IBM). IBM recast Concert at Think 2026 as a bundle over Instana, Turbonomic and related tools. Zylo and SoftwareOne cover SaaS. Alvarez & Marsal runs a 5-6 week benchmark-led IT cost-out, and Tech Mahindra markets 'guaranteed savings' to PE operating partners (snippet only; PDFs unreadable). Cognizant sells AI agents for application portfolio rationalization and halves assessment time. The gate imports the PE sponsor channel from 'The Middle' while that same gate downgraded The Middle because Ode ($1.5B) and OpenAI's Deployment Company (about $4B) contest the sponsor relationship. So the channel is asserted, not owned. After stripping out contested levers, the only differentiators left are 'we fund the engineering' and a 36-month tail. That is a balance-sheet position, not a moat, and the dossier's own pivot note admits the largest pool lies in the contested band.

The SAP custom-code wedge, the named first-10-customers play, is much softer than the gate credits. Rimini Street has committed to support ECC 6.0 and S/4HANA through 2040, with up to 90% maintenance savings claimed, which tells ECC customers they never have to convert. SAP's own ERP Private Edition Transition Option reportedly extends ECC to 2033 for RISE customers, and extended maintenance runs to 2030 for the rest, so there is no 2027 cliff. SAP gives away the analysis step (Custom Code Migration app, ABAP Test Cockpit, SCMON/UPL usage logging, per the dossier). Tessera Labs ($60M Series A, a16z) already does SAP upgrades with custom-code analysis. SIs bundle code cleansing into fixed-price S/4 conversions, so a Shrinker has to beat free tooling plus a bundled SI line item. Removing dead Z-objects saves little run cost unless a conversion fee or licence falls with it (the dossier found a self-reported cleanup that removed 17% of code after 14 months of usage data). The 'ECC enterprises with unreleased conversion budget' are the accounts the SIs and SAP are already working.

The incumbent's best counter-moves are cheap and legal, and they hit exactly where the Shrinker needs cooperation. The AMS vendor holds the ITSM data and the billing mechanics. Contracts carry confidentiality clauses, and sharing terms with an outside benchmarker can breach them (Hunton; in the worst case a claim of fundamental breach). Revenue minimums and volume bands can erase a ticket cut. The vendor can invoke these, drag out baseline resets to the renewal date, or simply offer the client a productivity credit to kill the engagement. Gainshare baseline fights are documented (Somerset/Southwest One, Sprint/IBM), and practitioner commentary says outsourcing gainshare 'rarely produces results'. The 'repeat-incident' lever works only on unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts, a small slice of the base. Meanwhile savings from retired apps arrive only at licence renewal, at decommission, or a year or more later when support staff are redeployed. So the Shrinker carries the engineering cost and the dispute risk up front, while the party it is cutting (the vendor) controls the evidence. The ESCO analogy does not carry over: the ESCO's customer finances the project and the savings are physical and metered, whereas here the Shrinker funds the work against a disputable, vendor-influenced ledger.

# C16 Dossier: Approved Buyer (sharpened pick: operator-led density consolidator of independent uniform and linen laundries, remedy-optional)

Pool P067 (US uniform, linen, workwear rental). Researched 2026-10-18 from about 45 searches and fetches, plus SEC filings pulled directly. "Gate" means the evidence-gate report for this idea. "Mine" marks my own arithmetic or judgment.

## 1. Bottom line

Verdict: weak. The sharpened pick is a real business but not a differentiated one. It is a standard private-equity roll-up of family laundries. Sellers exist, $100M of bought revenue is under 1% of the pool, and lenders are active. But at least ten funded buyers already do this, strategics pay synergy prices a financial buyer cannot match, and the FTC-remedy "option" that justified the original idea is worth close to zero in expectation. The revenue is bought, not earned: $100M of it costs about $130M of enterprise value (mine) and returns on that look like an ordinary 1.7x-2.7x equity multiple that depends on the exit multiple.

My cases for annual revenue in years 5-7: median $40M (gate said $45M, fair), realistic ceiling about $120M, remedy-driven $200M under 5% likely (mine). Overall score about 3.5/10.

## 2. Why-now: the trigger is real, the remedy is a lottery ticket with a bad payout

- **Status.** FTC Second Request issued 2026-06-11. Both parties certified substantial compliance 2026-10-02. A timing agreement bars closing before 2026-12-11 unless the FTC closes its investigation in writing. Cintas "expects" to close before year-end ([Cintas 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000723254/000072325426000047/ctas-20260831.htm)). Nothing public shows an FTC complaint, consent, or remedy proposal.
- **Cintas contractually declined remedies.** The merger agreement says Cintas "is not and will not be required" to sell or divest anything. In its December 2025 offer Cintas traded remedies for a $350M reverse fee and a duty to litigate. The outside date is 2027-01-10 and auto-extends twice by four months, to about September 2027 ([424B3](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000723254/000114036126020376/ny20069194x3_424b3.htm)). So a package exists only if the FTC forces it and Cintas then chooses to settle rather than fight.
- **Precedent.** Cintas/G&K (2017) cleared after eight months with no divestitures ([Jones Day](https://www.jonesday.com/en/practices/experience/2017/03/cintas-secures-antitrust-clearance-for-22-billion-purchase-of-gk-services)).
- **Signals for a remedy.** The FTC is interviewing independents and regionals. One source flagged high concentration in Nashville, Atlanta, Miami and Los Angeles, said buyers will be hard to find, and called Vestis an unlikely buyer (single source: [ION/Dealreporter, 2026-05-06](https://ionanalytics.com/insights/dealreporter/ftc-interviewing-competitors-in-unifirst-cintas-merger-source/)). A March analysis expecting 20-30% of branches to be divested ([Antitrust Intelligence](https://antitrust-intelligence.com/cintas-5-5-billion-acquisition-of-unifirst-likely-to-hinge-on-divestitures/)) has no named author and reads the $350M fee as a remedy signal, which the 424B3 contradicts. Treat it as low reliability.
- **Who gets remedy packages.** Established operators. The Ferguson FTC takes divestitures to an upfront buyer with "a long track record" ([Synopsys/Ansys, Mondaq](https://admin.mondaq.com/unitedstates/antitrust-eu-competition/1635112/return-of-the-remedy-first-ftc-merger-settlement-under-second-trump-administration-in-synopsysansys)). DOJ's UnitedHealth/Amedisys package (164 sites, about $528M revenue) went to BrightSpring and Pennant ([Healthcare Dive](https://www.healthcaredive.com/news/unitedhealth-amedisys-doj-settlement-merger/757086/)). Ascension/AmSurg sent seven centers in five metros to an existing operator and a physician group ([Cooley](https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2026/2026-08-31-ftc-requiring-divestitures-approves-final-consent-decree-in-ascensionamsurg-deal)). FTC's remedy study found whole-business buyers succeeded and staff scrutinize a buyer's financing and plan ([Crowell](https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/ftc-issues-report-evaluating-merger-remedies)).
- **Legal misframe.** There is no "pre-clearance." A buyer is approved inside a specific consent. A new vehicle with three ex-executives and committed equity is exactly the profile staff discount.
- **My odds.** Any divestiture about 25-30%. This platform named as a buyer, given a divestiture, about 10% (Alsco, Prudential and PE-backed operators are likelier). Joint about 3%. The practical checkpoint is 2026-12-11.

## 3. Competitors: confirmed, refuted, and new

The gate's "5+ funded buyers" is an undercount.

**Confirmed.**
- Alsco (family-owned): Churchill (Sep 2024), MacIntosh (Feb 2025), Topper (Jun 2025), Advanced Linen (Mar 2026) ([Alsco](https://alsco.com/news/alsco-uniforms-acquires-advanced-linen-service), [Pulse2](https://pulse2.com/alsco-uniforms-acquisition-of-linen-and-laundry-services-provider-advanced-linen-service-expands-california-presence/amp/)).
- Surge PE / White Plains Linen: over $50M, closed 2025-08-01, 15th platform, targets $4-35M EBITDA, Capital Southwest debt ([Jackson Walker](https://www.jw.com/news/result-surgepe-whiteplainslinen-investment/)).
- Falcon / Century Linen (2022): criteria $15-100M revenue and $2-10M EBITDA, PNC Mezzanine and Bank of America financing ([PE Professional](https://peprofessional.com/2022/07/falcon-buys-linen-platform-quickly-adds-new-facilities/)).
- Quintex / Mat Master, closed 2026-07-21 ([MLT Aikins](https://www.mltaikins.com/?p=32791)).
- UniFirst / Clean Uniform (2023, below).

**New, not in the gate.**
- Cornell Capital's PureStar bought Emerald Textiles (12 facilities), Jan 2026 ([Textile World](https://www.textileworld.com/textile-world/2026/01/purestar-announces-acquisition-of-emerald-textiles-creating-a-diversified-u-s-commercial-laundry-platform/)).
- Sterling Group bought HLSG from York, Apr 2026. HLSG then bought Crescent (Mar) and Texas Textile (May) ([TRSA](https://www.trsa.org/news/hlsg-acquires-texas-textile-services/), [Pulse2](https://pulse2.com/the-sterling-group-acquisition-of-healthcare-linen-services-provider-hlsg)).

Apollo and others arranged the financing ([Latham](https://www.lw.com/en/news/2026/09/latham-advises-on-financing-for-unitex-and-cvc-strategic-opportunities-strategic-partnership)).
- ImageFIRST (Calera): 25 acquisitions since 2018 and a $750M continuation fund ([Business Wire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20230614609951/en/Calera-Capital-Closes-$750-Million-Single-Asset-Continuation-Fund-for-ImageFIRST), [ImageFIRST](https://www.imagefirst.com/news-resources/news/calera-capital-acquires-majority-stake-in-imagefirst/)).

**Refuted or not found.**

- Elis's 2026 activity is Mexico (about EUR 5.5M revenue), not the US ([Le Soleil](https://www.lesoleil.com/communiques-de-presse/2026/08/10/elis-poursuit-le-developpement-de-son-reseau-en-amerique-latine-avec-une-nouvelle-acquisition-au-mexique-64LV6OF3P5EOHBSWGJMWH6QQDE/)). Pattern: most PE roll-ups are healthcare and hospitality linen. Buyers of industrial-uniform independents are strategics (Alsco, Cintas, UniFirst, Prudential) plus Falcon-type platforms. Falcon and Surge sit at $15M+ revenue, so sub-$15M targets face less PE competition but more strategic competition.

## 4. Bottom-up market and deal supply

- **Payers.** Sponsor and lenders fund; the independent's family owner signs the sale.
- **Pool.** TRSA claims a $50B+ North American industry with 2,500+ facilities ([TRSA](https://trsa.org/about-commercial-laundry-linen-services)). A TRSA state sheet cites $27+B for the US ([PA fact sheet](https://www.trsa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/022026_Pennsylvania-Fact_Sheet.pdf)). Independents hold about $11B (pool-file arithmetic; UniFirst FY25 revenue was $2.43B).
- **Universe.** Baird mailed its survey to about 500 independent firms and got 21 replies ([Baird 2Q26](https://www.trsa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Baird-2026-2Q26-Textile-Rental-Survey-Trends.pdf.pdf)). A TRSA article says about two-thirds of its independent members have revenue of $15M or less and all but three are family-owned; my read is the "nearly 175" it cites is the member base, not the industry ([TRSA](https://www.trsa.org/magazine-article/trsa-independently-owned-and-operated/)). An undated aggregator lists 329 firms in industrial launderers and 522 in linen supply ([mewayz 812332](https://data.mewayz.com/industry/812332), [812331](https://data.mewayz.com/industry/812331)). I found no revenue distribution.
- **Inference (mine).** Route-based targets above $8M of revenue are probably 100-200 firms, not the gate's "300." If the median target is $7-10M, $100M needs 10-15 deals.
- **Pace.** Best-in-class acquirers do about three deals a year (ImageFIRST 25 in eight years; Alsco four in 18 months). A new team doing 10-15 deals needs 5-8 years, so $100M is an outer-edge outcome for a new team, not the median.

## 5. Price evidence and willingness to pay

- **Sellers have alternatives**: Alsco, Cintas, a dozen PE platforms, family succession. Unlike a service with no budget line, the payer is not captive.
- **Demand backdrop** ([Baird 2Q26](https://www.trsa.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Baird-2026-2Q26-Textile-Rental-Survey-Trends.pdf.pdf)): renewal pricing +3.1%, new-account pricing still "net competitive," 12-month growth outlook +3.6% against a ~4% long-run average, and employment-driven add/stops at their weakest since 2024.
- **Margins** (TRSA 2026 report, 2025 data): median pre-tax 8.1%, industrial 18.1% (up 7.1 points), healthcare 4.5% (down from 10.3%), F&B linen 11.9% ([TRSA](https://www.trsa.org/news/industry-performance-report-industrial-segment-leads-profit-growth/)). Swings of 6-7 points in a year are a leverage risk.
- **Broker multiples are unreliable.** CT Acquisitions quotes 5-9x EBITDA and says Cintas/UniFirst priced at "about 8x run-rate EBITDA" before synergies ([CT Acquisitions](https://www.ctacquisitions.com/how-to-sell-a-uniform-rental-business/)). UniFirst's FY25 EBITDA was $324.9M ($184.5M operating income plus $140.4M D&A, [10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/717954/000119312525256222/unf-20250830.htm)). So $5.5B is about 16.9x trailing and 2.26x revenue; it is about 7.9x only if the full $375M of synergies is added.
- **Strategic comps.** UniFirst paid $300M headline (about $260M after tax benefits) for Clean Uniform with about $90M revenue: 2.9-3.3x ([Pulse2](https://pulse2.com/unifirst-acquiring-clean-uniform-for-300-million-details-unf)). Vestis is about 1.1x revenue and about 10x EBITDA (market cap about $1.87B per [MarketBeat](https://www.marketbeat.com/instant-alerts/price-vestis-nyse-vsts-stock-price-up-09-still-a-buy-2026-10-10/), net debt $1,205M per [Vestis Q3](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001967649/000162828026055485/vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm), FY26 EBITDA guide $310-315M).
- **Entry price (mine).** UniFirst D&A is 5.8% of revenue, so independents at 14-24% EBITDA margins and 5-9x give 0.8-2.0x revenue. The gate's 0.8-1.2x only fits the low-margin end. $100M of revenue costs $80-200M, central $130M.
- **Seller anchoring.** The 2.3x and 2.9x prints are a headwind. The gate is right here. Route-dense strategics that fold stops into existing routes can outbid a financial buyer.

## 6. Unit economics, capital and illustrative returns

- **Density gap is real, closing it is hard.** Cintas uniform operating margin is 24.1% ([10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000723254/000072325426000028/ctas-20260531.htm)). UniFirst earned 7.6% in FY25 and 3.6% in fiscal Q3 2026. Vestis earned a 12.2% EBITDA margin at 4.10x net leverage. Two national operators have not closed the gap, so "operator-led" is a claim, not a moat.
- **Capex.** UniFirst spent $107M in 39 weeks on $1.88B of revenue, 5.7% ([10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/717954/000162828026047621/unf-20260530.htm)). Consolidation plants cost money: Unitex's 130,000 sq ft Hartford conversion is about $9M for the building plus about $20M for fit-out ([Hartford Business](https://hartfordbusiness.com/article/medical-linen-company-eyes-30m-hartford-expansion/); sources show $21M or $30M). Prudential is spending $40-50M on a 100,000 sq ft cleanroom plant ([Cleanroom Technology](https://cleanroomtechnology.com/prudential-breaks-ground-on-100-000-sqft-cleanroom-laundry)). Budget $15-30M per metro hub.
- **Debt.** A broker guide puts lower-middle-market unitranche at SOFR plus 650-900 bps and leverage at 3.4x senior and 4.2x total for $10-50M EV deals, citing GF Data and Lincoln (unverified: [CT Acquisitions](https://www.ctacquisitions.com/debt-financing/)). Unitranche all-in yields were 9.33% in Dec 2025 ([Houlihan Lokey](https://cdn.hl.com/pdf/2026/hl-us-private-credit-market-newsletter-january-2026.pdf)).
- **Illustrative platform (mine).** Buy $100M of revenue at 1.3x ($130M) with 18% EBITDA ($18M, 7.2x). Add $10M of fees and integration, 4.0x debt ($72M at about 9.5%, $6.8M interest), capex $5.7M, tax $1.5M. Free cash flow is about $4M a year; equity is about $68M. In year 6, revenue is about $124M at 3.6% growth and debt about $42M.
  - Exit at 7x EBITDA (about 1.3x revenue): equity about $114M, 1.7x, IRR about 9%.
  - Exit at 10x (Vestis-like, about 1.8x revenue): about 2.7x, IRR about 18%.
  - Exit at a Clean-style 2.9x revenue: above 4x, but this needs a synergy buyer.
- **Exit buyers.** Alsco (family-owned; the idea file calls it capital-limited, which I could not verify), Elis (walked from US talks citing financial discipline, [BNN Bloomberg](https://bnnbloomberg.ca/investing/2024/10/04/elis-scraps-acquisition-talks-with-us-rivals-unifirst-vestis)), PE secondaries (CVC, Sterling and Calera show appetite), and Cintas/UniFirst only if the FTC allows. The merger arbitrage is real but not special.

## 7. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **HSR.** The 2026 threshold is $133.9M ([Orrick](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/01/HSR-Filing-Thresholds-Filing-Fees-and-Penalties-to-Increase-for-2026)). Independents' deals fall below it: no waiting period, but also no clearance, and the FTC can challenge after closing.
- **Environmental.** UniFirst's filings list consent-order cleanup sites (Woburn, Somerville, Springfield, Uvalde, Stockton, Williamstown) and accrue contingencies ([FY2019 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/717954/000156459019038460/unf-10k_20190831.htm)). A consultant notes former laundries often show solvent (PCE) conditions in Phase I reviews ([EEC](https://eecenvironmental.com/our-markets/industrial-laundries/)). Buy assets, run Phase I/II, and escrow. I found no remediation cost benchmark.
- **PFAS is not a forcing function.** EPA has finalized no PFAS effluent guideline ([CRS, 2026-09-30](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2026-09-30_IF12148_7411d6bc05ccbbc70ee4e9ed6f8ffb1569d3d172.html)), limits are local, and TRSA cites Michigan putting laundries at about 5% of PFAS waste ([TRSA](https://www.trsa.org/news/pfas-regulatory-update-risks-and-opportunities/)). The idea's "PFAS capex wall" should not be counted as seller motivation.
- **Labor.** TRSA reports operators worried about ICE I-9 audits and shrinking labor supply ([TRSA webinar](https://www.trsa.org/news/immigration-compliance-were-in-a-very-different-time/)).
- **Failure precedents.** Angelica went bankrupt in 2017 after losing its largest customer; its lender KKR bought it for about $160M by credit bid and cash ([Paul Weiss](https://paulweiss.com/practices/transactional/restructuring/news/kkr-completes-acquisition-of-angelica-corporation?id=24538)). Lighthouse Linen reorganized in 2026 and was recapitalized by Sundara ([Dealroom](https://dealroom.co/news/130863-lighthouse-linen-emerges-from-chapter-11-with-sundara-partners-control-i/)). Leveraged linen roll-ups can fail, which is also a source of distressed route books.

## 8. Upside-case assumptions tested

| Assumption | Finding |
|---|---|
| Remedy package of $150-300M revenue | Size unsourced. The only analogs went to established operators. About 3% joint odds (mine). |
| Vestis route book | Public, 4.10x levered, no sale process, EV about $3.1B. A $60-80M equity platform cannot bid. PE interest was 2024-25 ([Vestis Q3](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001967649/000162828026055485/vstsq3fy26earningsrelease-.htm)). |
| "Cintas cannot buy more" | Partly false (section 3). |
| Independents re-rated up by the UniFirst price | True, and it hurts the buyer. |
| 20-30% first-year leakage on divested books | Unsourced. The only retention datapoint is Vestis at -1.8% revenue and -4.5% pounds in a bad year. |
| Exit at 1.8-2.2x revenue | Plausible at 10-12x EBITDA only with margin over about 18% or a synergy buyer. Vestis shows 1.1x for 11.5% margins. |
| Operating bench of ex-regional presidents | Talent is moving: UniFirst's COO resigned Aug 2026 ([8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/717954/000119312526372350/d103272d8k.htm)). Non-compete exposure is untested. |
| $200M from independents alone | Needs 20-25 deals. At the best acquirers' pace of about 3 a year that is 7-8 years, beyond the 5-7 year window. |

## 9. Scorecard against the round-1 failure modes

1. **Small market:** passes. $100M is under 1% of the pool.
2. **Hidden incumbents:** fails. At least ten funded acquirers and four strategics are active, and several are larger.
3. **Wrong payer or no budget line:** sellers are real but not captive. Capital is available.
4. **Legal premise:** fails. "Pre-cleared" is not a mechanism, and Cintas has contracted around remedies.
5. **Price exceeds value:** at risk. Seller expectations are set by strategic prints.
6. **Why-now used up:** half. The consolidation wave is real, but the remedy window closes with the Dec 11 to Q1 2027 decision.
7. **Shrinking to survive:** yes. The pick dropped the remedy insight and became a generic roll-up.

# C14 dossier: Covenant Parks (pool P017, manufactured-home communities)

Dated 2026-10-18. About 50 searches, fetches and primary-file reads (NY park registry, statutes, term sheets, SEC filings). Tags: [S] read in a source this run; [D] my arithmetic from sourced numbers; [A] my assumption; [C] sources conflict.

## Bottom line

The gate's pick survives only as a capital-intensive real-estate sponsor, not as a scalable company, and its two best arguments are weaker than the gate said.

- **The gap is real but the beneficiary is the nonprofit.** I found no for-profit owner at scale that records a rent covenant. But every public tool that pays for covenants is built for co-ops and nonprofits, and the state tax breaks for sellers exclude for-profit buyers.
- **New York, the wedge state, already caps rents by statute.** RPL 233-b limits increases to 3% unless costs justify more, with a 6% ceiling. Maine charges large buyers $10,000 a lot. The covenant's differentiation is smaller than pitched in both.
- **The price risk is quantifiable.** A covenant buyer needing an 8% levered return bids about 6% to 24% below a market buyer, depending on the cap and expense growth. At the cap the pitch proposes ("lesser of CPI or 4%", so about 3% if CPI is about 3% [A]), the gap is 17-24%.
- **The $100M path is capital-bound.** It needs about 14,000 to 20,000 sites, $0.8-0.9B of assets and about $320M of equity. It also needs about 5% of all communities sold nationally each year, in a market where the typical park has 30-40 sites.

Verdict: wounded. Alive only if sellers, lenders and allocators pass the three tests at the end.

## 1. Competitors: confirmed, corrected, added

- **ROC USA (confirmed, bigger than the gate showed).** [S] 361 resident-owned communities in 22 states, 24,500+ sites, and it claims ROC lot rents rise about 1% a year against 7% in commercially owned parks ([ROC USA FHFA letter, 24 Jul 2026](https://www.fhfa.gov/sites/default/files/2026-07/ROC%20USA%20Duty%20to%20Serve%20Comment%20Letter%207.24.2026.pdf)). It has deployed $450M+ of mortgages since 2008, about $26M a year [D], and has a $47M acquisition pool backed by RWJF, JPMorgan and others ([ImpactAlpha](https://impactalpha.com/financing-resident-owned-mobile-home-communities-to-preserve-affordability/)). Its own page shows "59 of 68" against a 2026 goal; the unit is ambiguous [C] ([ROC USA](https://rocusa.org/our-impact/)).
- **New York MHAP (confirmed and more relevant than the gate said).** [S] For-profit and nonprofit owners are eligible. It lends at up to 3%, up to $60,000 a pad, and requires a recorded regulatory agreement. For existing homeowners it expects no more than a 3% lot-rent increase, and lot rents must stay at or below 40% of the 2-bedroom fair market rent ([HCR term sheet](https://hcr.ny.gov/manufactured-home-advantage-program-term-sheet-lender-addendum)).
- **Cascade Acres, NY is the closest analog to Covenant Parks.** [S] The residents' association used the new right of first refusal against a private-equity buyer. A local owner-operator, Brandon Montag, is "property manager and financier" and the association can buy him out. Financing was a $4.7M MHAP loan (20-year), a $420k village loan, a $1.6M bank loan and his equity ([Adirondack Daily Enterprise](https://www.dailygazette.com/ade/news/local_news/cascade-acres-makes-history/article_e4b455d1-3239-5955-a967-01d3f8ae03da.html), [HCR](https://hcr.ny.gov/news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-tenant-led-acquisition-essex-county)). So the structure exists, but as a one-off, subsidy-dependent deal. The bidder, Crown Communities, overbid a roughly $5.5M appraisal by $1.1M, about 20% ([WCAX](https://www.wcax.com/2025/08/06/lake-placid-residents-race-fend-off-sale-mobile-home-community/)). Unit counts conflict across sources (118, 124 and 165) [C].
- **Minnesota (verified, and the gate's claim holds).** [S] The Manufactured Home Community Redevelopment program accepts for-profit owners. It attaches a 25-year recorded Declaration of Restrictive Covenants, bars rent increases above 5% a year without approval, requires lot rents affordable at 115% AMI, requires approval to sell, and the covenant runs with the land ([Minnesota Housing FAQ, Sep 2026](https://mnhousing.gov/documents/45205/mhcr_rfp_faq/view)). A for-profit will take a recorded cap when a grant pays for it.
- **Public REITs (confirmed, still growing).** [S] Sun's Q2 2026 MH same-property revenue was +6.2%, NOI +8.8%, base rent $766 a site (+4.9%), occupancy 97.8% ([Sun 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000912593/000091259326000231/exhibit991pressreleaseands.htm)). ELS core MH base rent was reported +5.6% at about $956 ([MarketBeat summary](https://www.marketbeat.com/instant-alerts/equity-lifestyle-properties-nyseels-announces-quarterly-earnings-results-2026-07-22/), secondary). UMH same-store rental income was +8.7% in October ([UMH](https://s205.q4cdn.com/229505774/files/doc_news/UMH-PROPERTIES-INC--THIRD-QUARTER-2026-OPERATIONS-UPDATE-2026.pdf) via search summary). Their rent engine is intact, so they cannot offer a cap.
- **Private equity and funds (added).** OZ Impact Funds bought 21 communities with 2,740 pads for $100M in 2021, or about $36,500 a pad [D] ([IREI](https://irei.com/news/oz-impact-funds-acquires-21-strive-communities/)). Institutional buyers are reported at 23% of purchases, up from 13% in 2017-19 ([Propmodo citing PESP](https://propmodo.com/institutional-capital-floods-manufactured-housing-as-scarcity-meets-demand/), secondary). Sen. Hassan wrote to six corporate owners in Dec 2025 ([JEC](https://www.jec.senate.gov/public/index.cfm/democrats/2025/12/senator-hassan-presses-corporate-owners-of-mobile-home-communities-for-answers-on-affordability-and-resident-living-conditions)).
