## 2. Bottom-up market

- **Universe.** [S] More than 43,000 communities and 4.3M homesites ([Philadelphia Fed, citing MHI 2022](https://philadelphiafed.org/-/media/FRBP/Assets/Community-Development/Reports/manufactured-housing-communities-report-june-2023.pdf)). Lot rent runs from $766 a month at Sun and about $956 at ELS down to a Maine average of $479 ([Maine Public](https://www.mainepublic.org/business-and-economy/2026-08-18/new-data-shows-just-how-much-maine-mobile-homeowners-are-paying-to-rent-land-beneath-them)) and a 2021 national median of about $414 (same Philadelphia Fed report). The lot-rent pool is therefore about $25-40B a year [D]. The pool is large; the hard part is the part you can buy.
- **The wedge states are small-park states.** I analyzed New York's state registry ([data.ny.gov](https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/manufactured-home-park-registrations-beginning-2020)) [D]. In 2025 it lists 1,167 parks with 61,706 sites. The median park has 30 sites. Only 167 parks (14%) have 100 or more sites, and they hold about half the sites. 1,119 of 1,228 owner names (91%) own one park, using each park's latest 2020-25 record. Maine has 475 licensed communities and 19,348 lots, an average of 41 ([Maine Public](https://www.mainepublic.org/business-and-economy/2026-08-18/new-data-shows-just-how-much-maine-mobile-homeowners-are-paying-to-rent-land-beneath-them)). Pennsylvania is 62.5% medium (11-99 sites), 26.2% small and 11.4% large (Philadelphia Fed, above).
- **Annual supply is thin.** [S] Berkadia counts 460 communities sold nationwide in 2025 ([Berkadia](https://www.berkadia.com/lp/manufactured-housing-annual-report-2025/)); its coverage rules are not stated. In the NY registry, owner-name changes ran 32 in 2023 and 37 in 2024 out of about 1,075 matched parks. Only 27 changes in 2020-25 were parks of 100+ sites, about 5 a year [D]. Renames can inflate this proxy.
- **Conflict on the market.** [C] A [blog attributing the figure to Northmarq](https://rets.ai/blog/manufactured-housing-highest-yielding-asset-class) puts 2025 cap rates at 6.0%, down from 6.8%. Fannie Mae's own 2025 report says institutional-quality sales were on track for the lowest since 2015 through Q3 and cap rates rose after almost a decade of compression, with "credit-stressed exits by inexperienced or undercapitalized sponsors" ([Fannie Mae Duty to Serve 2025](https://www.fhfa.gov/document/d/dtsp/mh_tplp_1_nr_2025.pdf)). I trust Fannie. Northmarq's Q1 2026 median price was $58,400 a space, +12% ([Northmarq](https://northmarq.com/insights/insights/manufactured-housing-transaction-activity-rises-year-over-year-q1-2026)). Berkadia's +1.4% effective rent growth conflicts with Northmarq's 6.8% and the REITs' roughly 5%, probably on definitions [C].

## 3. Demand and willingness to pay

- **Residents do not pay for the covenant.** They already pay lot rent. The payers are (1) the state, through MHAP and Minnesota money; (2) the seller, through a price discount; (3) LP capital, through a lower return. Only (1) has a documented budget line.
- **Sellers accept discounts mainly for non-financial reasons and with tax help that Covenant Parks cannot use.** Vermont co-ops paid $3.6M against a $5M ask and $1.84M against $2.4M, where families wanted the park kept affordable ([VPR](https://www.vermontpublic.org/vpr-news/2015-11-24/proud-new-land-owners-a-mobile-home-park-success-story), [Seven Days](https://www.sevendaysvt.com/?p=107764), via search summaries). Minnesota gives a seller a credit of 5% of the sale price only for sales to co-ops, 501(c)(3)s and resident-representing nonprofits ([Minn. Stat. 290.0694](https://revisor.mn.gov/statutes/2023/cite/290.0694/pdf)) [S]. Maine exempts up to $750,000 of capital gains on sales to resident-owned communities and housing authorities ([Maine Senate](https://www.mainesenate.org/transformational-new-laws-to-protect-residents-of-mobile-home-communities-take-effect/)) [S]. HUD's FHA 223(f) community loan excluded for-profit owners at launch in 2024 ([MHI](https://www.manufacturedhousing.org/news/new-hud-and-fha-community-loan-program-fails-to-include-for-profit-community-owners/)) [S].
- **The one documented contested price went the other way.** A private-equity bid beat the appraisal by about 20% at Cascade Acres. Maine's first right-of-first-refusal sale (Hidden Circle) was a $1M purchase of 31 homes, about $32,000 a lot, with $310,000 from the state fund ([Gov. Mills](https://www.maine.gov/governor/mills/news/governor-mills-celebrates-purchase-hidden-circle-mobile-home-park-jay-residents-2026-08-18)) [D].
- **Resident and political demand is real.** Washington capped manufactured-home lot-rent increases at 5% in May 2025, and owners sued in Jan 2026 ([OPB](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/01/22/manufactured-home-park-owners-sue-washington-rent-cap/)). Pennsylvania HB 1250 (a lot-rent cap) passed the House in June 2025 and awaits the Senate ([PA Lt. Gov.](https://www.pa.gov/ltgovernor/newsroom/lt--gov--austin-davis-highlights-policies-to-make-housing-more-a)). A search summary, not opened, says SB 746 (right of first refusal) cleared committee in June 2026.
- **Not found:** any seller, allocator or lender stating they will pay for a for-profit covenant. Owner age data for communities does not exist in what I found. "Sellers aged 65+" is an untested hypothesis.

## 4. Unit economics (my model, not a sourced figure)

Setup [A]: $7,000 revenue a site, 40% expense ratio, $250 a site capex, 6.5% going-in cap, 65% LTV at 6.4% interest-only, 10-year hold, 2% buy and 1.5% sell costs. The 6.4% debt is inside the 6.2-6.9% agency range quoted by brokers on [6 Oct 2026](https://www.apartmentloanstore.com/fullerton/california/apartment-loan-rates) and [Greystone](https://www.greystone.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Small-Rates_2026.08.11.pdf), against a 10-year Treasury of 4.69% in August.

| Rent growth / expense growth | Levered IRR (exit +50 bp) | Levered IRR (exit +150 bp) |
|---|---|---|
| Market: 5.5% / 3.5% | 19.1% | 17.3% |
| Cap 4% / 3.5% | 14.5% | 12.5% |
| Cap 4% / 5.0% | 12.3% | 10.1% |
| CPI-linked ~3% / 3.5% | 10.8% | 8.5% |
| CPI-linked ~3% / 5.0% | 7.8% | 5.1% |

- **The cap itself is survivable. The squeeze between the cap and expense growth is the risk.** A Spokane Valley owner cited utilities up about 22% as a reason to sell ([Spokane Public Radio](https://www.spokanepublicradio.org/regional-news/2026-01-26/washington-sued-rent-control-mobile-home-parks-sell)).
- **Price tolerance.** Solving for an 8% levered return, a covenant buyer's maximum price is 6% below a market buyer needing 12% (cap 4%, expenses 3.5%). It is 13% below at 5% expense growth, and 24% below with CPI-linked rent and 5% expenses. Against a 15%-hurdle private-equity buyer the gap is -16% to +5%. REITs buying at "low-4%" caps (an AI-generated summary of Sun's Q1 call, low authority) are not catchable.
- **Not modeled, all negative for returns:** the resident equity glide path, the formula-priced buyout in years 7-10, a thinner exit buyer pool, and reassessed property tax.
- **Leverage is roughly neutral.** Debt costs 6.2-6.9% against entry caps of 6-7.5%.

## 5. Capital needs

- **Equity and assets.** 14,300 sites at the model price is about $870M of assets and $320M of equity at 65% LTV [D]; the gate said $290M. I found no data for an alternative.
- **Agency debt does not fit the niche.** Freddie's MHC loan wants "existing, stabilized, high-quality and professionally managed" communities, a $1M minimum, five pads, and a sponsor with two years of MHC operating experience who owns another MHC ([Lument term sheet, 6 Jul 2026](https://www.lument.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Freddie-Mac-Manufactured-Housing-Community-Loan_7.6.26-1.pdf)). Fannie lowered its minimum from 50 to 40 pads in 2025 (Fannie report above). The small, rural, deferred-maintenance parks that sellers over 65 own are the least agency-eligible. Fannie's tenant-protection pricing is small: a search summary of its [2019 memo](https://multifamily.fanniemae.com/sites/g/files/koqyhd161/files/migrated-files/content/announcement/lm1901.pdf) gives a 7.5 bp nonprofit discount, and broker [term sheets](https://lument.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Fannie-Mae-Manufactured-Housing-Term-Sheets.pdf) say tenant-protection pricing carried a 10% payment guaranty. Current basis points are unconfirmed.
- **Exit financing.** Residents buying out need ROC-type debt. By the time buyouts arrive, about $125M of purchases a year for 22 parks is roughly 4.8 times ROC USA's historical annual deployment of about $26M [D].
- **No allocator evidence.** Nuveen's impact housing fund seeded with $250M from TIAA invests in rent-restricted and naturally affordable housing, with no target return published ([ConnectCRE](https://www.connectcre.com/stories/nuveen-secures-250m-for-impact-housing-fund/)). It shows the buyer type exists, not that it accepts this deal.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- **New York RPL 233-b [S]** ([text](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/RPP/233-B)). Increases may not exceed 3% unless justified by operating expenses, taxes or capital costs. Increases are irrebuttably justified up to the resident's pro-rata share of costs, and a 6% ceiling applies unless a court grants a temporary hardship. Parks under an affordability regulatory agreement are excluded. The pitch's "lesser of CPI or 4%" adds little in New York.
- **Right of first refusal.** New York's runs 140 days from notice and needs more than 50% of homeowners (NCLC [2026 white paper](https://www.nclc.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026.09_White-Paper_Summary-of-Manufactured-Home-Laws.pdf)). In Maine residents must match price and terms and have 90 days to finance. Residents can match a Covenant Parks bid, so it can lose any deal in these states.
- **Maine fee [S]** (10 M.R.S. 9094-B, [text](https://legislature.maine.gov/legis/statutes/10/title10sec9094-B.html)). Buyers pay $10,000 a lot unless they and affiliates, including any 20% holder, have net worth under $75M. The statute as amended by PL 2025 c. 688 says $75M; the press and the original law said $50M [C]. At 41 lots, the fee is about $410,000 a park, or about 30% of a $32,000-a-lot price [D]. A fund over the net-worth line loses Maine.
- **Lender conflict.** Freddie's term sheet says "Leases cannot contain options to purchase pad site." A pre-granted resident right to buy must sit outside the leases and be cleared with the lender. Fannie's section 603.05 was blocked to me; this is unverified for Fannie.
- **Unverified legal risks.** I did not find whether resident "equity credits" create securities or installment-sale (contract for deed) characterization. The gate cited New York and North Carolina rent-to-own statutes; treat it as a counsel item.

## 7. Is the why-now real?

Partly. The pressure is real: right-of-first-refusal laws, the Hassan inquiry, Washington's cap, Pennsylvania's bill, 5-9% REIT rent growth and Fannie's "softening NOI" report. But policy money and tax breaks flow to co-ops, nonprofits and housing authorities; for-profits are the regulated party (Maine's fee) or excluded (FHA 223(f), the Minnesota and Maine seller credits). The shock helps ROC USA first.

The legal duty cannot be moved, but the tail can, and nobody will insure it. The official Awaab's Law phase 2 guidance says landlords using contractors "retain full responsibility" for compliance (s8.5). It says alternative accommodation is at the landlord's expense (s9). It says courts can award damages and the tenant's legal costs (s13.4). It calls it "unacceptable" to assume a hazard is the tenant's "lifestyle" (s2.4), and says cooking, bathing and drying laundry are unlikely to be a breach. A hot-spot provider therefore cannot carve tenant behaviour out of a five-year repeat-repair guarantee. The landlord will demand a back-to-back indemnity for uncapped damages, decant costs and claimant costs (uncapped until at least Oct 2028). The clocks also make cost variable by law: 24 hours for emergencies, 10 working days to investigate, 5 to make safe, and new investigation clocks after any "material change". A capitated fee that wants fewer visits sits against a statute that mandates them, and rationing visits is exactly what the Ombudsman and regulator punish. The tail has no insurer (insurers exclude gradual damage; most housing-condition claims are uninsured, per the gate), and an extended guarantee sits on the FSMA insurance perimeter edge.

The capital and cost-trend maths do not close. The dossier models GBP20-40M of risk capital by year five for a business that its closest incumbents run at a 5.7% margin (Mears FY25). Sector repair spend is GBP9.7bn over the last 12 months and forecast at GBP11.1bn for the next, so a fee set at 80% of trailing cost is roughly 100% of true cost within about two years. Break-even needs a 44% cut in recurring cost if the provider funds the fixes. The only measured cut found is 25% on repeat visits, from analytics alone, at one landlord (a vendor case). Landlords cannot fund the root-cause capex themselves: RSH puts sector cash interest cover at 59% in the quarter to June 2026 and says recovery is "slower than previously forecast", so the provider must pre-fund works on assets it does not own. Fixed-price repair contracts also have an exit history. MPS left a GBP10M, 5-year Angus contract (4,000+ homes) after under a year, citing labour and materials volatility. Lambeth paid to exit Fortem early and re-let at higher cost. ForHousing cited rising repair numbers and costs under a 2017 fixed arrangement. I could not confirm the pricing mechanism in the Angus or Lambeth cases.

The technical premise (a root-cause fix that stays fixed) and the data premise (clean, address-level cost data) are both unproven. Mould recurrence is documented: a Zehnder-commissioned survey (vendor-sponsored) found 51% of landlords said mould came back after treatment; Thurrock minutes record a councillor saying it recurred in a third of properties within two years; Ombudsman decisions show ventilation systems found switched off. Ranking homes by trailing three-year cost needs reliable property-level data. RSH reported the average landlord had surveyed only 75% of homes in five years (to March 2024), and about three quarters of C3/C4-graded landlords had weak stock-condition coverage or poor understanding of their homes. The landlords with the worst hot-spots are therefore the ones with the weakest data, which is adverse selection for a fixed-fee price. The landlord's trailing spend is the schedule-of-rates price (contractor margin included, with rate-building a flagged risk), not the true cost. The ICO has said housing bodies must pass a necessity test before sharing tenant health data, which constrains a cross-landlord dataset. The kill test (top 5% of homes carry at least 15% of spend) has still not been run by anyone: no published top-5% split exists.

The why-now is misaligned with the entry window. Phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026, but the landlord response in 2027-29 will be compliance process and the already-awarded contracts, not new risk-transfer structures. The reformed Decent Homes Standard adds a damp-and-mould criterion (Criterion E) applying from 2035, with no requirement to prioritise the worst homes or start earlier, so there is no forcing function in the startup's window. Only 4% of landlords call themselves very prepared, which favours the frameworks and law-firm tooling already selling to them. The second payer line (disrepair claims) is small and concentrated in London councils: about GBP25M across 78 councils and 3 associations in 2024.

Bundling: Livin (about GBP200M, 10 years, single lot, TAC-1 alliance covering responsive, voids, adaptations, compliance, planned, retrofit, cyclical; award notice 27 Feb 2026), Thurrock (GBP240M), Winchester (GBP56.7M, scope names disrepair and damp-and-mould work types), PfH GBP480M and Riverside GBP657M frameworks. Insourcing: Teign Housing is ending a 10-year Ian Williams contract in April 2027 so it has 'more control over how we work' [V]; Grand Union, Uttlesford, Basildon, Ashford, Cheshire West. The signer (FD/Director of Assets, then board) would be paid roughly a 20% saving on the cohort (about GBP560 a home, about GBP1.1M on 2,000 homes, under 0.5% of a 40,000-home landlord's turnover [A]) while the landlord stays the s10A duty holder with the full legal, Ombudsman and reputational tail on its most vulnerable, most litigated homes. The Ombudsman's Hyde investigation blamed failure to oversee contractors. That is a bad risk/reward for a career-risk-averse buyer. The fee also draws on three budget owners (responsive, disrepair/legal, capital) [A], so there is no single owner with a budget line and a burning need. Demand shown in the dossier is for works and software (Mobysoft GBP97-276k a year, Wigan GBP2M, InCommunities GBP3M), never for capitation. Absence of any carve-out precedent after about 10 targeted searches is consistent with buyers not wanting it, not only with a gap.

SALES CYCLE AND QUALIFICATION GATES MAKE THE VOLUME PATH UNREACHABLE FOR A NEWCO. Even a plain, incumbent-favoured whole-stock deal is slow: Thurrock went pipeline notice May 2025, tender notice July 2025, estimated award Sept 2025, actual award 19 May 2026, start 1 July 2026 (about 14 months, award slipped about 8) [S]. A novel carve-out adds pre-procurement engagement, baseline data sharing, board approval, and a Procurement Act flexible procedure even for a 500-home pilot (about GBP1.1M a year, over the GBP207,720 threshold). PfH itself says 'the rate of adoption from pilot to business as usual remains low' and 'procurement processes are slow, especially for new or unproven suppliers' [V]. Search summaries of Find a Tender notices report turnover thresholds of about 2x annual contract value (Livin GBP40M on GBP20M a year; a 2023 council notice GBP33M) [S, notices returned HTTP 403 so unverified]. A 2,000-home cohort is about GBP4.4M a year, so about GBP9M turnover or a parent guarantee; a newco has neither, and reinsurers want 12-24 months of loss data that only a signed contract produces. That is a chicken-and-egg loop on capital, references and data. The $100M path needs about 17 signed landlords in about 6-7 years; at 18-24 months per sale [A] and a 20-30% win rate [A], that is roughly 60-80 bids against only 45-55 reachable payers [dossier A], many locked into price-per-property incumbents to 2031-36. SHED is a pilot door, but the PfH quote above is exactly why pilots do not convert.

PRICING BASIS AND MARGIN DO NOT SURVIVE CONTACT WITH THE BASELINE. The fee is 80% of trailing three-year cost, a pre-Awaab baseline. RSH Q1 2026 shows repairs and maintenance spend of GBP9.7bn over the last 12 months against GBP11.1bn forecast for the next 12 (+14%) [V]. It is aggregate spend, so it includes volume growth, but a capitated provider carries exactly that volume risk. Phase 2 (30 Nov 2026) adds seven clocked hazard categories and phase 3 follows, so true cost runs above the fee in about 2 years without indexation, which fixed-price buyers resist (ForHousing exited a 2017 fixed arrangement over rising repair number and cost). The dossier's own model needs a 44% cut in recurring cost to break even if the provider funds the fix, and 40-60% for the claimed 12-18% margin; the only measured result is a 25% cut in repeat visits from analytics alone at Gloucester (vendor case), which gives about -24% margin. The buyer's saving is also thin (about 20%) and unverifiable, because the trailing baseline is noisy: Housemark's emergency-hazard medians jumped from 6.3 to 35.8 per 1,000 homes in a month from recording changes. Disputes over baseline are the default outcome. It needs GBP20-40M of risk capital by year 5 [dossier A] to earn a few points of margin, which is a poor trade against Mears's 5.7% on GBP1.1bn.

THE TAIL IS UNCAPPED, UNHEDGEABLE AND CONTROLLED BY THIRD PARTIES, AND THE COHORT IS WHERE IT CONCENTRATES. Hot-spot homes are the same homes that generate disrepair claims, and claimant costs are uncapped until at least Oct 2028. Hackney paid GBP1M compensation plus GBP3.6M claimant fees on 508 claims, about GBP9k a claim; the FOI sample average works out at about GBP2.8k (GBP25M / 8,999 claims) [dossier S, my division]. Nationally 25-40k claims a year, half of them in the worst 5% of homes, implies about 6-9% of cohort homes claiming a year [A]. At 5% of 35,000 homes that is 1,750 claims, or GBP4.9-15.8M, which is 6-20% of the GBP77M fee and erases the margin. The provider cannot control claim volume (claims farming, CMCs, SRA concerns about cold calling and door-knocking), nor settlement strategy (SRA-regulated counsel under the landlord's control), nor access: North Yorkshire's page says 'most companies acting on your behalf will advise you not to allow access' during claims [V]; Flintshire alleges solicitors advised tenants to refuse repair access [V]; Southern Housing v Emmanuel [2025 EWCC 58] reportedly holds there is no forced entry [S] and the law is split. So the provider guarantees root-cause outcomes in homes whose occupants are advised to block the fix while the repeat-visit clock keeps running. No stop-loss or damp-and-mould cover product was found, insurers exclude gradual damage, and the guarantee wording sits on the FSMA 'insurance' line. The landlord cannot transfer the statutory liability, so it is buying a discount, not protection.

THE CONTRACT ERODES ITS OWN REVENUE, SO LTV IS SHORT, AND THE CLAIMED MOAT IS NOT THERE. The fee is indexed to cost. If the provider succeeds (a 40-60% cut), the landlord resets or re-tenders at lower trailing cost; at 60% the fee falls from about GBP2,240 to about GBP1,340 a home (-40%) [A]. A 5-10 year term does not give switching costs, because the Procurement Act forces re-competition at expiry and the buyer, now holding the five-year dataset and fixed assets, can insource (Teign is the live precedent of a 10-year outsourced contract ending in insourcing). Counter-positioning against 'visit-based' primes is weak, since primes already sell price-per-property (St Albans, Thurrock, Dacorum) and carry hot-spot cost, and would treat a carve-out as cherry-picking and probably breach exclusivity. The cornered-dataset claim is weak because Mobysoft already holds a claimed 7M-job multi-landlord dataset and sells for under GBP300k a year. The kill test (top 5% of homes carry 15% or more of spend) is still unrun, and the best public data (Thurrock 2013-14: 27% of homes had 5+ repairs) shows broad concentration, not a sharp 5% tail, which weakens the 'target the top 5%' pitch and raises the cohort's scatter and cost to serve (24-hour and 5-day Awaab clocks across scattered homes). Dossier-realistic range is about 3 landlords and $13M median, 10 landlords and $58M upside, against the $100M needed. What survives is a small remediation-services or subcontract business, not a $100M company.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Any of the following, in order of weight. (1) Two or three finance-director-signed letters of intent from landlords with 25k+ homes to carve out at least 1,000 worst-cost homes each on a capitated, multi-year basis, with written confirmation that their current repairs contracts permit a cohort carve-out (no exclusivity clash) and that a Procurement Act route exists that a newco can qualify for. That would show a funded buyer, a named signer and a way in. (2) Job-level data from at least three landlords showing the top 5% of homes carry 25% or more of repair, disrepair and compensation spend (the unrun kill test), together with a pilot of at least 100 homes that measures a 45% or greater sustained cut in recurring cost against an agreed, indexed baseline (not analytics-only cuts like Gloucester's 25%). (3) A written stop-loss or reinsurance quote that covers the repeat-repair and disrepair-claim tail at a price leaving at least 10% margin, plus FCA perimeter advice that the structure is not insurance. (4) A prime or large balance-sheet partner willing to be the named qualifying entity and to white-label or co-bid, with a revenue split that leaves the newco at least 12%. (5) Evidence that buyers pay for this kind of risk transfer today, for example a landlord tender that creates a worst-homes lot with outcome-based pricing, or a signed contract where a contractor carries claims-cost risk and still earns a margin. Without (1) and (2), the volume case of about 17 landlords is a hope, not a market.

objections: The strongest incumbent already sells the adjacent product and already holds everything the entrant would need to borrow. Wates launched 'Healthy Homes' in April 2024, a dedicated damp-and-mould and disrepair-reduction service, delivered with its own labour, with six customers already signed. Wates says it manages repairs for 500,000+ homes across 65 social landlords. The gate and the dossier both missed this. Mears has said regulation is creating new damp, mould and condensation service lines [S], and it is winning 10-year total-asset deals: Rooftop is GBP15M a year for 7,000 units (about GBP2,143 a home) and Birmingham is GBP45M a year for 11,500 units (about GBP3,913 a home), both covering far more than repairs. The hot-spot fee the idea wants (about GBP2,200 per costly home) is about what Mears is already paid per average home for everything. A landlord on price-per-property can tell its prime to fix the root causes at no extra fee. A landlord on visit-priced contracts can write a hot-spot lot or pain/gain schedule into its next tender or an amendment. The likely incumbent response is cheap: add a gain-share schedule, bundle sensors and analytics, and price it as part of the existing contract. The incumbent wins because it already has the job-level data, the vans, the tenant access and the landlord relationship. The entrant would depend on a landlord handing over data and a cohort carved out of the incumbent's contract, and on the incumbent not objecting. Scattered single homes across a patch give the entrant no route density, so the likely end state is subcontracting to the prime at prime-level margins (Mears guides to 5.0-5.2% for FY26, 5-6% medium term) rather than 12-18%.

The claimed moats do not hold against what exists today. (a) 'Cornered' cross-landlord loss dataset: Wates sees job data on 500,000+ homes and Mobysoft claims 7M+ jobs, so any entrant's cohort data would be smaller than incumbents' for years. Identification of hot homes is also cheap or built in: Mobysoft RepairSense sells for about GBP97k-276k a year with a measured 25% cut in repeat visits at Gloucester City Homes, Switchee lists plans from GBP99 a home [S], Sureserve's Property MOT already bundles a damp-and-mould survey and ventilation check into the annual gas visit, and Croydon's NEC dashboard flags properties with multiple repair reports [S]. A landlord can buy the easy 25% for a few pounds a home and give the fix to its existing contractor. That leaves the capitated entrant only the harder savings, and the dossier's own model needs a 44% cost cut to break even when the provider funds the fix. (b) Counter-positioning against visit-based pay: the primes are not all visit-paid. Price-per-property is a standard option in procurement toolkits (Winchester's questionnaire, Thurrock, St Albans), so 'the responsive contractor never proposes the fix' is a problem PPP contracts already pay to solve. (c) Reinsurance relationships: no stop-loss product was found anywhere, so this is an unbuilt dependency, not a moat.

The 'guarantee' is table stakes at component level, so it does not differentiate, and the part that is not already insured is the part the entrant would be left holding. Insurance-backed 20-year guarantees on damp work are specified in housing association tenders (ClwydAlyn, Wales) [S] and backed by PCA/GPI. EnviroVent gives a 10-year warranty on its Atmos positive-input-ventilation (PIV) unit, and Airtech guarantees mould treatments for three years against recurrence. What those guarantees exclude is gradual damage, tenant behaviour and access, and that residual is what a five-year repeat-visit guarantee would have to carry. Evidence that access and behaviour bite: a Thanet KPI report shows damp-and-mould remedial works in target falling from 87.9% to 67.1% in Q1 2026/27, attributed to access for follow-on appointments [S, page blocked, contractor not named]. The legal duty also stays with the landlord (Brabners) [S], so the landlord keeps the clock and the claim risk and has little reason to give control of its worst homes to a thinly capitalised newcomer.

Capitated and fixed-price repair deals have a record of eroding or failing, which both deters buyers and punishes the seller. MPS gave notice on a GBP10M, 5-year, 4,000+ home Angus contract within a year, citing labour and price shocks. Lambeth exited its Fortem repairs contract about two years early and the replacement costs more. ForHousing/Cheshire West cited rising repair cost and volume. Exeter's price-per-property contract saw exclusions rise from 30% to 36% of spend in 2024/25 [S], so scope disputes and carve-outs hollow out the 'one fee covers everything' promise. The idea prices at 80% of trailing cost while sector repairs spend is rising 13-14% a year, and it is a balance-sheet business needing an estimated GBP20-40M of risk capital. The managed-care analog is Cano Health's Chapter 11 on capitated risk. The prime that does best here, Mears, still earns about 5%.

Landlords with genuine hot spots have better alternatives than a startup, and the doors into them are mostly shut. (a) Insource: Hyde (a G15 landlord that took a Housing Ombudsman special investigation) 'brought our repair service in-house', and Basildon, Ashford and Cheshire West have also insourced. (b) Dispose or regenerate: the dossier shows boards sell or regenerate negative-NPV homes (Southwark, Haringey). (c) Use free capital: the Warm Homes Social Housing Fund offered just under GBP1.15bn across 138 projects with at least equal landlord match funding [S], won by incumbents such as Mears (about 5,000 retrofits), so fabric and ventilation fixes on the worst homes can be grant-funded instead of paid for by a capitated provider. (d) Procurement vehicles already cover disrepair: the PfH GBP480M framework has 12 firms on all four lots, including PE-backed roll-ups (Axis and CLC under H.I.G. with unitranche financing, Cardo) plus Equans and United Living, and 75 suppliers in total. Riverside's GBP657M disrepair framework (12 regional lots) is reported to run to about 2029. A newcomer must subcontract to a winner, so the competitor is also the channel.

objections: The sharpened pitch (operator-led, family-to-family alternative to the nationals) is already being run by better-credentialed operators, and the dossier missed the closest one. Wildman Business Group (family-owned, Warsaw IN) has nine locations, 13,500+ customers and 500 staff. It announced Springfield Laundry on 2025-10-13 with succession as the stated reason. It keeps acquired names, branding and sales teams, and says it wants to be the 'alternative succession plan to large nationals' for independents. Alsco closed Churchill (Sep 2024), MacIntosh (Feb 2025), Topper (Jun 2025) and Advanced Linen (Mar 2026). The Advanced Linen co-owner said he and his partners 'carefully chose' Alsco as the company they trust with their customers. Behind them sit at least ten funded buyers (Surge, Falcon, Quintex, PureStar/Cornell, Sterling/HLSG, CVC/Unitex, Calera/ImageFIRST). KPMG told TRSA in Feb 2026 that strategic buyers dominate most deals to add route density. A new vehicle with three hired executives, no closed deals and no reference customers is the least credible bidder a family owner will see. Strategics fold stops into existing routes, so they outbid it on the best targets. Cintas paid $164.5M cash for FY26 tuck-ins that added about 0.6% (~$62M) to revenue growth, roughly 1.3x-2.7x revenue by my arithmetic given part-year effects. UniFirst paid 2.9-3.3x for Clean Uniform. The platform therefore inherits adverse selection: targets with no strategic fit, deferred capex or key-person risk. 'Density' also cannot be bought. A metro has one to three independents, and the first deal in each metro has no density while the incumbent there values it at a synergy price.

The retention device is cheap to copy and, as designed, damages the economics. Prudential already publishes a 12-month pricing guarantee on all rental items, and Alsco's whole acquisition pitch is 'we keep the customer relationships'. A price lock is a contract term, not a moat. The 24-month price lock plus month-to-month option also undercuts the underwriting. Baird's 2Q26 survey shows renewal increases averaged only 1.5-2.0% over the prior two years (+3.1% now), and new-account pricing is still net competitive (index 45.5). On the dossier's own illustrative book ($100M revenue, $18M EBITDA, $72M debt), 2-3% annual cost inflation against frozen prices cuts EBITDA 18-28% in 24 months, to $14.7M or $13.0M. That takes leverage from 4.0x to about 4.9-5.5x (my arithmetic). Dropping the evergreen contract also removes the recurring-revenue feature that unitranche lenders and exit buyers pay for. The '20-30% first-year leakage' that justifies the device is unsourced. The only retention datapoint I saw (unverified, from a summary of Vestis materials) is rolling 12-month retention of about 92-93%, which is roughly 7-8% churn.

The strongest respondent, Cintas+UniFirst, has no reason to spare the platform, and the remedy option is nearly worthless. The combined company would hold about 40% of the pool with $375M of targeted synergies. Cintas grew uniform organic revenue 7.6% in FY26, while Baird's independent respondents expect 3.6%. That sample is 21 replies from about 500 firms, so it is survivor-biased and probably optimistic. The dossier's illustrative model assumes the platform grows 3.6%. Cintas keeps buying independents outside overlap metros regardless of the deal. The 10-K says acquisitions have been a meaningful growth source, so 'Cintas cannot buy more' is false. objections: The seller-preference edge is asserted, not evidenced, and the evidence points the other way. The sharpened pick says it wins on 'seller preference and post-deal retention', but sellers name a different criterion: trust to look after their customers. In the one 2026 deal I could open, Advanced Linen's co-owner said they 'carefully chose Alsco' as the company they trust to take care of their customers. Alsco is a fifth-generation family firm that has done four deals in 18 months. A newly formed vehicle has no track record, and its three ex-regional presidents come from the competitors the sellers fight every day. CT Acquisitions (a buy-side broker) says a competitive process with more than one strategic 'almost always lifts the price', and the strategic prints are far above the platform's 0.8-1.2x revenue: UniFirst/Clean Uniform at 2.9-3.3x, Cintas/UniFirst at 2.26x. A seller who sells to the lowest bidder because of a rep equity pool is the opposite of how the evidence says owners behave. The cheap test (20 owner calls) has not been run, so the pitch is a hypothesis.

The retention features that define the pitch destroy the asset being bought. The 24-month price lock and the month-to-month option contradict how this industry is valued and financed. CT Acquisitions says converting handshake and short-term customers to multi-year auto-renew contracts with minimum-volume terms is 'the biggest multiple lever'. It puts route-thin, short-contract operators at 5-6x EBITDA versus 7-9x for deep multi-year bases. On the dossier's illustrative $100M-revenue, 18%-EBITDA, $130M purchase, 5-6x exit EBITDA is $90-108M, below cost. My arithmetic, assuming 3% cost inflation: with no renewal price increases for two years, EBITDA falls from $18M to about $13M. That is a 22-35% cut depending on whether the foregone increase is the 2.0% of the past two years or the 3.1% in Baird's 2Q26 survey. Net debt of $72M then sits at about 5.5x EBITDA against 4.0x at close. The exit assumption of 1.8-2.2x revenue is about 10x EBITDA at an 18% margin, which is above the top of the broker range for route-dense multi-year books. The price-lock and month-to-month feature also differentiates nothing: a pipeline-trades blog (unverified) says regional players already write 1-year contracts and price 15-20% below Cintas.

Entry price and earnings quality make the deals hard to close and the returns thin. Sellers will anchor on 2025 earnings, and TRSA's 2025 data show the industrial median pre-tax margin jumped 7.1 points in one year to 18.1% (from about 11.0%). Healthcare fell to 4.5%, its lowest in nine years, and mixed fell 4 points to 7.8%. A seller prices the peak year while a lender and sponsor underwrite mid-cycle, which opens a bid-ask gap that a first-time buyer cannot close with a retention story. Baird's 2Q26 survey (21 responses from about 500 independents) shows no tailwind to underwrite. Wearer add/stops are at their weakest since 2024 (index 36.4), 67% of respondents met revenue expectations and none beat them, new-account pricing is still net competitive, and the 12-month growth outlook is +3.6%. Renewal pricing of +3.1% is above the 1.5-2.0% of the past two years, so the growth driver is price, and the platform has promised to forgo it. The dossier's own model yields about a 9% IRR at a 7x exit and about 18% only at 10x. Corporate overhead on a young platform is also unmodeled. Assuming $3.5M of overhead (my number), that is about 12% of revenue at $30M. The dossier's median case of $40M of revenue, about 3-4 deals, leaves the platform sub-scale for years.

The 'customers' who fund and source the deals (sponsor and lenders on one side, owners on the other) are both hard to acquire at the stage that matters. On the funding side, the plan to line up $150-250M of equity commitments in the first 90 days before any deal is not supported. McGuireWoods (Jan 2026) says capital providers want to be engaged 'well before a live transaction' and that rollover, earn-out and holdback terms are hard to revise after the LOI. The Gen II/Buyouts 2026 report calls the emerging-manager market 'barbell' and difficult. That same McGuireWoods piece also says the binding constraint is deal quality rather than money, so the capital risk is real but not fatal. On the sourcing side, the vendor blogs I found put cold-owner reply rates at about 1-5%, and say 30-50% of 'proprietary' closed deals come via intermediaries. CT Acquisitions says off-market sales close in 90-180 days against 9-18 months for broker listings and that brokers charge 8-15%. The dossier counts about 100-200 route-based targets above $8M, and ImageFIRST did 25 deals in about 8 years. Ten to fifteen deals at $10M each is a 5-8 year build even for a best-in-class acquirer, so the $100M case does not fit the 5-7 year window for a first-time team. These sourcing numbers are vendor-sourced and weak, but nothing contradicts them.

The end customers can leave at the moment of ownership change, and the plan to consolidate plants raises that risk. Alsco's own contract page notes that an acquisition does not automatically change contracts, but it prompts customers to read their termination and renewal clauses. Management teams in this sector name key route-rep turnover as the main attrition risk (CT Acquisitions), and the platform's rep equity pool is a standard fix that Alsco and Cintas already have the scale to match. After deal 3 the plan closes duplicate plants into one hub-and-spoke plant per metro. That lengthens routes and changes delivery days for the very customers the price lock is meant to hold. Lighthouse Linen's 2026 reorganization is a nearby example of customers hedging during ownership stress: an industry outlet said it must rebuild trust with healthcare and hospitality clients. The 20-30% first-year leakage figure in the idea file is the author's own unsourced estimate, and I found no sourced leakage rate for any uniform-rental acquisition either. That means the retention case, on which the whole pitch rests, has no data behind it. Finally, the 'why now' remedy trigger is gone as a plan: as of October 2026 nothing public shows a divestiture (ASI, 10-Q), and Cintas contractually declined to accept remedies, so the sharpened pick has no differentiated demand-side reason to exist beyond a generic PE roll-up that at least ten funded buyers already run.

objections: The remedy option is dead on mechanism and timing, so the sharpened pick is just a generic roll-up. Cintas proposed in Dec 2025 that it not be required to engage in antitrust remedies, and the merger agreement obliges both sides to defend any challenge in court. The outside date is Jan 10, 2027, extendable to Sept 10, 2027. That makes clearance or a litigated fight more likely than a negotiated divestiture package. As of the latest filings and trade coverage (Oct 2026) no divestiture or consent is mentioned anywhere; the only reporting is one anonymous Dealreporter source saying buyers will be hard to find. Earliest closing is Dec 11, so the platform has about 53 days to get committed equity, a lender, officers and FTC-credible financing in place. It has none of them today. The obvious buyers of any package are established operators that already close tuck-ins: Alsco (four deals in about 18 months), Prudential, and PE platforms such as ImageFIRST, PureStar, Sterling's HLSG and Unitex/CVC. Cintas picks the buyer and staff scrutinize the buyer's financing and track record (dossier sourcing). A new vehicle with three ex-executives is the profile staff discount. The dossier's own odds put this platform being named a buyer at about 3%.

Capital and returns do not clear a sponsor's bar, and the exit is circular. The dossier's own model gives about $4M a year of free cash flow on about $68M of equity, with about a 9% IRR at a 7x exit and about 18% at 10x. Only a synergy buyer pays 10x or more (UniFirst paid 2.9-3.3x revenue for Clean Uniform). The synergy buyers are Cintas, which has just taken on UniFirst and an open-ended FTC process, and UniFirst. Elis walked from US talks, and I found no completed 2025-26 sale of a PE-backed uniform or linen platform to validate the 1.8-2.2x revenue exit. Calera's ImageFIRST went into a $750M continuation fund in 2023 instead of a clean sale. Raising $60-80M of first-close equity, or $150-250M of commitments, for a first-time operator team with no assets runs against the market. PitchBook shows experienced managers took 88.1% of PE fundraising dollars in 2025 and first-time funds are having a harder time. McGuireWoods says fundraising cycles are longer. Houlihan Lokey headlines a more than tenfold rise in stress among the smallest private-credit borrowers since 2023 and puts sub-$100M-EBITDA default at 3.0% by size and 3.6% by count in 2Q26. A lender-blog source says institutional lenders want $2M or more of EBITDA, while a $10M-revenue target at 14-24% margins is only $1.4-2.4M.

Deal flow is crowded and probably adversely selected, and the entry price rests on a broker's marketing range. At least ten funded acquirers are active, and strategic tuck-ins (Cintas, UniFirst, Alsco, Prudential) can fold stops into existing routes and outbid a financial buyer. Seller anchors are the 2.3x and 2.9-3.3x prints. No 2025-26 closed revenue or EBITDA multiple for a sub-$15M independent was found; the 0.8-1.2x assumption comes from CT Acquisitions' unsourced 5-9x range, which the broker itself labels its own point of view. The sellers who are available are plausibly the weaker ones, given the succession gaps and capex questions the pitch cites. Baird's 2Q26 survey, which drew 21 replies from about 500 firms, shows add/stops at 36.4 (weakest since 2024), no respondent above revenue expectations, 3.6% expected growth, and new-account pricing still net competitive. TRSA's margin data warns of buying at a peak: industrial median pre-tax margin jumped 7.1 points to 18.1% in one year, mixed fell 4 points to 7.8%, healthcare fell to 4.5% (lowest in nine years), and the overall median is 8.1%. IBISWorld sees profit at about 7.6% by 2031.

Operator-led is a claim, not a moat, and the team has to be hired before the money exists. UniFirst earned a 3.6% operating margin in fiscal Q3 2026 and Vestis runs 4.1x levered after S&P cuts to BB- (2024) and B+ (2025), and an S&P research update titled as a further cut to B. Two national operators with real scale have not closed the density gap with Cintas's 24.1%. The plan needs three ex-regional presidents on signed offers and an equity pool before any raise, which means funding salaries with no revenue. Their covenants are untested. Massachusetts caps non-competes at 12 months with garden-leave pay of at least 50% of base. Georgia presumes covenants of two years or less reasonable. Cintas lost Cintas v. Perry (7th Cir. 2008), but that was an Illinois-law case where the covenant was overbroad, and outcomes are state-specific. Labor friction is live: Teamsters ULP strikes at Vestis in Indianapolis (July 13, 2026) and a strike authorization in Las Vegas, plus I-9 audit risk flagged in laundry trade guidance.

Inherited liabilities and antitrust exposure are treated as footnotes but raise cost and diligence burden on small deals. Industrial laundry sites carry solvent (PCE) contamination risk, and CERCLA makes current owners strictly liable; California's AmeriPride Sacramento order is an example. New since the dossier: on Aug 18, 2026 the D.C. Circuit upheld EPA's PFOA/PFOS CERCLA hazardous-substance designation, which widens the all-appropriate-inquiries diligence for any plant that discharges to sewer or sludge. I found no laundry-specific liability case, so this is a diligence cost and an unknown, not a proven loss. Asset purchases of unionized plants can trigger successor withdrawal liability to multiemployer pension funds; the Seventh and Ninth Circuits are more willing to impose it than the Second. Deals under the $133.9M HSR threshold get no clearance, and the FTC can challenge them after closing. The 2023 Merger Guidelines target serial acquisitions, and the USAP/Welsh Carson consent imposed prior-notice duties on non-reportable deals. The FTC is already interviewing independents about concentration in Nashville, Atlanta, Miami and Los Angeles, so a roll-up buying overlap-metro independents invites that attention. Consolidation hubs cost $15-30M per metro (dossier), which is out of scale with $10M-revenue targets.

result.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any one of the first three would move this from serious to manageable.
(1) Named, committed equity of $60-80M or more from an anchor LP or family office that will back a first-time operator team before any deal is signed, with a lender term sheet at 4x or more on a platform of about $10M-revenue targets.
(2) Credible reporting or an FTC filing showing Cintas will divest a package of $150M or more of revenue to a buyer not yet named, plus a written signal from Cintas's counsel or the FTC staff that a new, financed vehicle with a hired operating bench qualifies as an upfront buyer.
(3) Three or more closed 2025-26 sales of sub-$15M independents with disclosed multiples at or below about 1.0x revenue and 6x EBITDA, or three signed IOIs from owners aged 60 or older at those terms from an operator-led buyer with route-rep equity.
Supporting evidence that would help: a completed 2025-26 sale of a PE-backed uniform or linen platform to a strategic other than Cintas or UniFirst at 10x EBITDA or more; the TRSA margin distribution showing a median sub-$15M independent EBITDA margin of 14% or more across 2023-25; legal confirmation that the three ex-regional presidents are free of enforceable covenants in their states; Phase I/II and pension diligence on two real targets showing no inherited environmental or withdrawal liability; and the Dec 11 to Q1 2027 window passing with a divestiture package announced, which would show the option was real after all."

objections: NOBODY WITH A BUDGET PAYS FOR THE COVENANT, AND SELLERS PICK CERTAINTY OVER MISSION. Residents pay nothing extra, so the payer has to be a seller taking a discount, an LP taking a lower return, or a state subsidy. The dossier's own model puts a covenant buyer 6-24% below a market buyer. The documented seller behavior points the other way. At Fox Run (Lewiston, Maine) the sellers took $2.6M from BoaVida over a $2.64M resident-co-op offer. The Cooperative Development Institute says that in the failed Maine attempts 'every offer was greater than the offer from the capital equity firm', and the co-ops still lost on terms and speed. Cascade Acres (NY): the private-equity bidder overbid a roughly $5.5M appraisal by about 20%. Matthews (2026) says well-marketed assets reportedly sold 8-15% above initial expectations. If a co-op bidding at or above price loses, a covenant bidder 6-24% below price loses worse. The sellers who do accept a haircut go to nonprofits, who get tax help a for-profit cannot use (the Minnesota 5% credit, the Maine $750k exemption, a reported federal 75% credit that excludes for-profit buyers). No seller, broker or allocator has been found who says they will pay for a for-profit covenant. The only budgeted payer found is the state, and that money is built for nonprofits and co-ops. I would not call this fatal, because nobody has tested it with real bids. But the $100M case needs this customer to exist in volume, and the evidence leans against it.

THE CLOSEST REAL ATTEMPT ALREADY DIED ON THE SAME CAPITAL POOL, AND THE DOSSIER MISSED IT. The dossier says it found no for-profit acquirer or fund raised on this thesis. It missed Integrity Community Solutions (ICS). ROC USA, the most credible operator in the space, formed ICS as a subsidiary to buy and stabilize parks, planned a roughly $30M fund, and funded it with $2M of seed. It completed one deal, an 84-unit California park financed with a $3.4M loan. ROC's board voted to shut it down in 2025 'amid a shifting political and regulatory environment'. The founder, Paul Bradley, disputes that a capital shortfall killed it, and ROC's HUD-grant/DEI exposure is a confounder. ICS had no rent covenant, and it was an interim owner that sold to co-ops, so it is not identical. The signal still holds. A team with an existing impact-LP base (Ceniarth, RWJF and JPMorgan back ROC's separate acquisition loan pool) got one deal in about a year. Its stated plan for that deal, filling vacant lots with new homes, 'has not come to fruition' because low-income households cannot afford to buy homes. Bradley's next effort is now being incubated at the Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, which makes it a philanthropy-backed competitor for the same impact capital. Two sources disagree on ICS's founding date (2023 vs 2024). Neither says how much of the $30M was actually raised.

THE SIGNER WHO FUNDS IT HAS NO PRODUCT SLOT FOR A FIRST-TIME SPONSOR, AND THE COVENANT CAPS THE EXIT. The pitch needs a pension or insurer investment committee to write $50M+ tickets at 7-8% levered into an unproven strategy. The dossier's own IRR table gives 10-15% for a fixed 4% cap and 5-8% for a CPI-linked cap with 5% expense growth, against 17-19% for a market owner. That falls between the impact lane (ROC-type capital at around 1%) and the commercial lane (value-add and core funds, Apollo's $850M fund, Brookfield's reported >$10B Yes! Communities deal, Invesco's Homestead platform). Debut-fund evidence is dated or weak: the Preqin figure that 91% of firms under $1B AUM won't back first-time real estate funds is from 2015, and a 2025 vendor blog says first-time funds take about 22 months to close and only 34% hit target. Freddie's term sheet also wants a sponsor with two years of MHC operating experience. The exit is worse. A recorded 10-year covenant plus a formula-price buyout to residents in years 7-10 leaves nonprofits and co-ops as the buyers. ROC deploys about $26M a year against the $125M a year this plan buys, so exit demand is about 4.8x short. Restricted-rent real estate in general sells into a narrow, mission-driven buyer pool (an Idaho LIHTC sale record: six offers narrowed to two). With revenue pinned to a cap and costs floating (a Spokane Valley owner cited utilities up about 22%), the LP's downside is a squeeze with a thin buyer pool.

THE GO-TO-MARKET MATH REQUIRES WINNING ABOUT 5% OF ALL NATIONAL PARK SALES WHILE BIDDING BELOW THE AUCTION. About 460 communities sold nationally in 2025 (Berkadia), and the plan needs about 22 parks a year (about 4.8%). Park size makes it worse: the NY median is 30 sites and the Maine average is 41, with lot rent around $5-5.75k a site. That is roughly 420-580 parks for $100M, each needing its own diligence, septic/well review and lender process. Broker-run sales are seller-fiduciary auctions that reward the highest, cleanest bid, and Frank Rolfe says about half of parks bought over 25 years came from brokers. The only channel where a covenant pitch could win on non-price grounds is off-market direct mail. A mailing hit rate of about 1% (a 99% failure rate) is anecdotal operator folklore, and mid-size professional operators and institutions already hunt the same owners. ROFR deals add 140 days (NY) or 60-90 days (Maine) plus a matching right, and the dossier itself notes residents can match a Covenant Parks bid, so it can lose any deal in those states. Allocator fundraising adds a likely 18-22+ months before the first closing. The dossier's 30-day tests can falsify the pitch quickly, but a $100M outcome would take 6-8 years after a fund close.

THE DIFFERENTIATION AND THE FINANCING HOOK ARE ERODING FROM BOTH SIDES. Where rent is capped by law, the covenant is redundant: NY RPL 233-b limits increases to 3% (6% ceiling), Washington has a 5% cap, and PA HB 1250 would cap at 4%. Where it is not capped, no payer exists (objection 1). New York's MHAP already lends at up to 3% for a recorded 3% cap, so a for-profit is competing with subsidized money. Maine's $10,000-per-lot fee exempts only buyers with net worth under $75M, so a roughly $290M-equity fund pays it, loses Maine, and pays about 30% of a roughly $32k-a-lot price. The one financing hook, Fannie's tenant-protection mission pricing, is worth only a few basis points (the dossier found 7.5 bp from a 2019 memo, unconfirmed today). MHI said in 2022 that the vast majority of owners already follow tenant-protection terms. FHFA's Duty to Serve replacement rule (91 FR 37848) drops the prescribed-activity framework and extra credit, and says only that it 'updates the approach to determining affordability for manufactured housing communities'. MHI's July 2026 letter asks that community financing not favor particular ownership structures. How the final rule treats MH communities is unclear, but the pricing edge could disappear by the expected 1 Jan 2028 effective date. Freddie's term sheet also bars purchase options in leases, so the resident right to buy needs a financeable structure outside the lease, which adds cost and time.
